title: Accountants and auditors
rationale: Core tasks center on examining financial records, tax computation, risk analysis, report writing, and advisory recommendations—predominantly digital, cognitive, and language-based work where AI and RPA already automate routine bookkeeping and data processing while assisting higher-level analysis. Demand elasticity is moderate because lower costs can unlock more professional services for small businesses and individuals, yet regulatory mandates (audits, tax filings, SEC requirements) and structural caps keep overall volume from expanding dramatically. This combination produces restructure: the occupation persists but shifts heavily toward judgment, client advisory, and AI oversight, so non-adapters face displacement while adaptable workers thrive.

title: Actors
rationale: Actors’ core daily work requires physical presence, live or on-camera embodiment of characters, emotional authenticity, memorization under performance conditions, and real-time collaboration with directors and cast—tasks that remain predominantly non-digital and presence-dependent; AI currently assists only peripheral elements such as script analysis, digital extras, or voice synthesis and is not yet close to replacing high-quality human performance across theater, film, and live venues. Demand elasticity is high because entertainment output is strongly cost-constrained: dramatically cheaper production would expand the volume of films, series, ads, games, and experiential content, creating more total roles even after some substitution. With only moderate disruption to core tasks, the occupation remains resilient overall—AI alters industry economics and certain subfields without reshaping the fundamental human performance work.

title: Actuaries
rationale: Actuaries' core work—compiling data, statistical modeling of risk probabilities and costs, designing policies, calculating reserves, and generating reports—is almost entirely digital, quantitative, and language-based, placing it squarely in AI's path; modern ML and generative tools already accelerate forecasting, scenario testing, and documentation. Demand elasticity is low because the volume of insurance products, regulatory filings, and enterprise risk assessments is constrained by market size, regulation, and fixed institutional needs rather than analysis cost; cheaper actuarial output does not unlock 10x more policies or risk studies. High disruption combined with limited demand expansion therefore implies significant headcount contraction as AI absorbs routine modeling and junior analytical tasks.

title: Administrative services and facilities managers
rationale: Core duties blend knowledge work (policy recommendations, energy analysis, records management, compliance planning) that AI already assists via predictive tools and automation with irreducible physical presence for facility inspections, staff supervision, on-site maintenance oversight, and emergency response, producing only moderate disruption. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper/faster management could unlock some latent demand for better energy efficiency, security, and records practices across more organizations, yet overall headcount remains constrained by the relatively fixed stock of buildings and firms. The combination keeps the occupation resilient: AI changes tools and peripheral efficiency but does not displace the human-centered core.

title: Adult basic and secondary education and ESL teachers
rationale: Core tasks such as lesson planning, content creation, assessment, progress monitoring, and adaptive instruction are predominantly cognitive and language-based, already materially assisted by AI tools and adaptive platforms for basic skills and ESL, placing the occupation in the high-disruption range even though real-time classroom facilitation, cultural sensitivity, and student motivation still require human presence. Demand elasticity is moderate because lower costs and greater personalization can unlock additional participation among immigrants, low-literacy adults, and workforce-development programs, yet expansion is constrained by declining GED need from higher high-school graduation rates, public funding limits, and a finite population requiring these credentials. The combination produces restructuring: the role shifts toward AI-orchestrated facilitation, high-touch coaching, and resource navigation, so adaptable teachers remain valuable while pure content-delivery headcount contracts.

title: Advertising sales agents
rationale: Core tasks such as client research, proposal and media-kit preparation, sales analytics, contract drafting, and personalized outreach are predominantly digital/cognitive and already materially assisted by AI tools, while relationship-building and closing remain human but are heavily augmented; this places the role in the high-disruption band. Demand for advertising sales labor is largely inelastic because total ad budgets and the shift to programmatic/self-serve platforms constrain volume; 10x productivity gains therefore translate into fewer agents rather than proportionally more advertising sold. The combination of high disruption and low elasticity produces net headcount contraction, consistent with the already-projected decline.

title: Advertising, promotions, and marketing managers
rationale: Core tasks—market research analysis, campaign strategy and planning, creative evaluation, pricing/customer acquisition strategy, and media decisions—are predominantly cognitive, digital, and language-based, with AI tools already generating copy/designs, optimizing media buys, and surfacing insights, placing the role firmly in the high-disruption band similar to other managers. Demand elasticity is high because marketing output is not fixed; dramatically cheaper and faster strategy development unlocks latent demand from smaller firms, enables continuous experimentation and hyper-personalization, and expands total campaigns and market-entry efforts rather than simply shrinking headcount. The combination produces an augment outcome: each manager oversees far more output with AI, supporting stable or growing employment as overall marketing activity scales.

title: Aerospace engineering and operations technologists and technicians
rationale: Core duties mix substantial physical hands-on work (building/maintaining test facilities, fabricating and installing parts and instruments, operating wind tunnels and assembly) with digital/cognitive tasks (calibrating computer systems, recording data, running simulations, quality monitoring). AI already assists the latter via better simulation tools, anomaly detection, and automated analysis, but cannot replace the real-world presence, mechanical skills, and safety-critical physical operations required, placing disruption in the moderate mixed range. Elasticity is moderate because lower cost and faster testing would unlock additional design iterations, small-satellite programs, electric aircraft, and drone development in a capital- and regulation-constrained industry, expanding total output without fully offsetting productivity gains. Net effect is therefore resilient: AI reshapes peripheral analysis and simulation work but leaves the occupation’s physical core intact.

title: Aerospace engineers
rationale: Aerospace engineering is predominantly knowledge work centered on design, simulation, analysis, optimization, and evaluation of complex systems; AI already accelerates CFD, generative design, structural optimization, digital twins, and data-driven testing, materially changing core cognitive tasks even if physical prototypes, certification, and manufacturing oversight remain human. Demand elasticity is moderate because lower engineering costs and faster iteration unlock more commercial space projects, drone applications, fuel-efficient redesigns, and small-satellite constellations, yet expansion is capped by capital-intensive manufacturing, materials, regulatory certification, and government budgets. High disruption combined with only moderate elasticity means the occupation persists but the skill mix shifts heavily toward AI-augmented workflows, systems integration, and higher-level judgment, displacing those who do not adapt.

title: Agricultural and food science technicians
rationale: Disruption is moderate because core duties mix physical, presence-required work (sample collection on farms/plants, operating equipment, maintaining sterile labs, examining specimens) with cognitive tasks (analyzing results, preparing reports/charts); AI already aids data analysis and imaging but cannot replace hands-on protocols or real-world agricultural settings. Elasticity is moderate as cheaper/faster testing and research support would unlock some additional R&D into climate-resilient crops, food safety, and processing efficiency, yet overall demand remains constrained by physical production volumes, regulatory testing minima, and fixed research budgets rather than expanding unboundedly. The net effect is resilient since disruption stays at or below the moderate threshold, so AI primarily augments peripheral analysis without reshaping the occupation's core.

title: Agricultural and food scientists
rationale: Agricultural and food scientists perform predominantly knowledge-based research involving experimental design, statistical analysis of large datasets, genetic and soil modeling, product formulation, and scientific writing/communication, all areas where AI tools already provide material assistance via predictive analytics, simulation, literature synthesis, and generative design, even as some lab and field validation remains human-led. Demand elasticity is high because needs around climate adaptation, food security, resource efficiency, and novel product development are currently constrained by research costs and timelines; dramatically cheaper/faster science would unlock substantially more funded projects, breeding programs, and food innovations across industry and government. Productivity gains are therefore absorbed by expanded output rather than pure headcount reduction, with workers who master AI tools producing far more impact. This fits the augment category as high disruption pairs with high elasticity.

title: Agricultural engineers
rationale: Disruption is high because core work centers on computer-aided design of equipment/systems, environmental modeling, optimization, and AI/geospatial integration—all cognitive/digital tasks where generative design, simulation, and analysis tools already materially accelerate output—while physical testing, site oversight, and construction supervision remain human-required. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper/faster engineering unlocks more precision-ag, waste, climate-resilience, and automation projects for a broader set of farms and processors, yet expansion is capped by capital costs of physical implementation, farm economics, and regulatory constraints rather than pure digital scalability. This produces restructure: the occupation persists with expanded project volume in some segments, but the skill mix shifts heavily toward AI orchestration, validation of generated designs, and interdisciplinary client work, displacing those who do not adapt.

title: Agricultural workers
rationale: Core tasks are overwhelmingly physical, manual, and outdoors—planting, harvesting, herding, cleaning pens, and operating machinery in unstructured environments—so AI and robotics assist mainly via precision tools, sensors, or autonomous equipment rather than replacing daily labor. Demand for agricultural output is highly inelastic; cheaper or faster production does not lead society to consume dramatically more food or livestock products, so productivity gains historically and prospectively shrink headcount. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate, the occupation stays resilient even as some tasks become more automated.

title: Air traffic controllers
rationale: Core ATC work mixes digital monitoring, cognitive decision-making, and radio communication with an absolute requirement for real-time human presence, judgment under uncertainty, and regulatory accountability; AI already supplies decision-support tools (conflict prediction, trajectory optimization, NextGen) that raise productivity but leave final clearances and emergency handling with controllers, placing disruption in the moderate range. Demand for controllers is tightly coupled to flight volume, which expands only gradually and is constrained by airport capacity, airspace rules, and safety certification; productivity gains therefore translate mainly into higher traffic handled per controller rather than large headcount growth. Because disruption remains at or below 6, the occupation is classified resilient: AI reshapes tools and throughput but does not displace the core human role.

title: Aircraft and avionics equipment mechanics and technicians
rationale: Core work is predominantly physical and hands-on—diagnosing then repairing/replacing aircraft components with tools, climbing, inspecting in hangars or on airfields under strict FAA rules—so AI assists only knowledge portions like predictive diagnostics, data interpretation, manuals, and records rather than reshaping the occupation. Demand for maintenance is largely fixed by fleet size, flight hours, and regulatory schedules; cheaper/faster work could modestly expand air travel and thus aircraft numbers but is constrained by airports, airspace, manufacturing, and overall travel demand, limiting elasticity. With disruption only moderate, AI augments periphery without displacing the human presence required for safety-critical physical tasks, leaving the occupation resilient.

title: Airline and commercial pilots
rationale: Core tasks center on real-time physical control of aircraft, takeoffs/landings, emergency response, and cockpit presence under unpredictable conditions, so AI mainly augments peripheral cognitive elements like flight planning, system monitoring, weather analysis, and decision support rather than displacing the human pilot. Demand for flights expands modestly with lower costs via leisure travel and e-commerce cargo, yet remains constrained by airport capacity, airspace limits, regulation, and finite passenger needs, preventing productivity gains from unlocking large latent volume. With only moderate disruption, the occupation stays resilient as AI tools assist without reshaping the essential human-in-the-loop role.

title: Animal care and service workers
rationale: Core tasks—feeding, cleaning enclosures, grooming, exercising, restraining, and hands-on training—are almost entirely physical and require unpredictable real-world presence with live animals, so AI is limited to peripheral aids such as camera-based monitoring, digital record-keeping, or scheduling. Demand for pet and animal services already expands with rising pet ownership and humanization of pets; cheaper or faster care would unlock some additional boarding, grooming, and training volume, but growth remains constrained by the finite number of animals and the need for individual physical attention. Because disruption stays low, the occupation is resilient: AI touches the edges without reshaping daily work or displacing headcount.

title: Announcers and DJs
rationale: Core tasks for broadcast announcers and radio DJs—script writing, research, content selection, commentary, and even voice delivery—are heavily language- and knowledge-based, with AI already enabling automated DJs, synthetic voices, and generated programming as noted in BLS projections; party DJs face lower disruption due to live presence and audience reading but still use AI for mixing and selection. Demand is inelastic because radio/TV listening time and advertising slots are not expanding with cheaper production (stations consolidate instead), while live events are constrained by the fixed volume of weddings, parties, and clubs rather than cost. This combination of high disruption and low elasticity produces net headcount contraction, matching the projected overall decline.

title: Anthropologists and archeologists
rationale: Disruption is moderate because core work mixes physical fieldwork (excavation, on-site observation, interviews, artifact handling in remote or rugged conditions) that requires human presence with cognitive tasks (data analysis, pattern recognition, report writing, advising) where AI already assists via GIS, image classification, literature synthesis, and drafting. Elasticity is low because demand is constrained by research funding cycles, federal budgets, academic slots, and regulatory compliance tied to construction volume rather than price; cheaper analysis unlocks only limited extra corporate cultural consulting or more thorough surveys. The net effect is resilient as AI reshapes peripheral knowledge tasks without displacing the occupation's essential real-world presence requirements.

title: Arbitrators, mediators, and conciliators
rationale: Core work centers on real-time facilitation of dialogue, reading emotional cues, building trust, and remaining neutral in charged interpersonal settings, which requires human presence even if sessions can be virtual; AI already assists peripheral cognitive tasks such as document review, legal research, precedent analysis, and drafting settlement language, producing moderate overall disruption. Demand for dispute resolution is only moderately elastic: lower cost and speed would shift more cases from litigation into ADR and unlock some currently unresolved small or community disputes, yet the underlying volume of conflicts is structurally limited and does not expand without bound. Because disruption remains moderate, the occupation is resilient—AI reshapes preparation and analysis but leaves the essential human mediation role intact.

title: Architects
rationale: Architects' core work is predominantly knowledge-based—client requirements gathering, conceptual design, CADD/BIM modeling, specifications, code compliance analysis, and documentation—all of which generative AI and advanced BIM tools already accelerate and are rapidly improving, even while site visits, physical construction oversight, and high-stakes aesthetic/functional judgment still require human presence. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster design unlocks more custom work for smaller clients, renovations, and sustainability optimization plus expanded architect roles across the project lifecycle, yet overall volume remains constrained by construction costs, land, regulations, and macroeconomic building demand rather than exploding. High disruption paired with only moderate elasticity therefore produces restructuring: the occupation persists but shifts heavily toward AI orchestration, client strategy, and complex judgment, displacing those who cannot adapt.

title: Architectural and engineering managers
rationale: Architectural and engineering managers perform predominantly cognitive and knowledge-based work—detailed project planning, budgeting, resource allocation, quality oversight, and coordination—which AI already assists via generative design tools, automated scheduling, predictive analytics, and reporting, yielding high disruption even though interpersonal leadership and staff supervision remain human. Elasticity is moderate because productivity gains let managers handle larger teams or more concurrent projects and overall A&E activity may expand with cheaper engineering, yet demand is still bounded by capital budgets, regulatory timelines, and physical infrastructure needs rather than scaling unboundedly. The combination produces restructure: the occupation endures but the skill mix shifts sharply toward AI fluency, strategic oversight of automated systems, and managing hybrid human-AI teams, so non-adapters face displacement while adapters thrive.

title: Archivists, curators, and museum workers
rationale: Core tasks mix physical hands-on work (object handling, restoration, exhibit installation, cleaning artifacts) with cognitive elements (cataloging, authentication, research, digital records management, exhibit design), so AI already assists metadata generation, image analysis, digitization, and content creation but cannot replace the need for human presence, tactile skill, and public interaction. Demand is constrained by institutional budgets, physical space, public interest, and funding models rather than pure cost; cheaper AI-enabled work unlocks more digitization and smaller-scale projects but does not create unbounded expansion in museums or archives. Because disruption remains moderate, the occupation is resilient overall, with AI reshaping peripheral digital workflows without displacing the core role.

title: Art directors
rationale: Art directors' core work of visual concepting, style development, design review, and layout direction is predominantly cognitive and digital, with generative AI already producing high-quality image variations, mockups, and style options that materially accelerate ideation and production. Client communication, team leadership, budgeting, and final creative judgment still require human presence, keeping disruption high rather than maximal. Demand elasticity is high because dramatically cheaper and faster visual direction unlocks latent demand for more advertising campaigns, digital content, packaging variants, personalized media, and productions as cost barriers fall. This combination means AI multiplies output per director while expanding total market volume enough to support stable or growing headcount for those who adapt.

title: Assemblers and fabricators
rationale: Core tasks center on physical positioning, hand-tool assembly, and real-world manipulation of parts, with only secondary cognitive elements like reading schematics or visual QC; AI already aids via computer vision inspection and collaborative robots but leaves the bulk of manual work intact, placing disruption in the moderate range. Elasticity is low because cheaper, faster assembly enables limited reshoring and volume gains yet faces structural ceilings from overall goods demand and market saturation, so productivity improvements primarily shrink headcount rather than expand total work. The combination yields a resilient outcome: AI reshapes peripheral processes and efficiency without displacing the occupation’s physical core.

title: Athletes and sports competitors
rationale: Core tasks center on physical athleticism, real-time competition, training, and bodily performance that AI cannot execute or substitute, confining AI to peripheral aids like video analysis, biomechanics, opponent scouting, and training optimization. Demand for professional athletes is structurally capped by fixed league rosters, team counts, stadium capacity, and broadcast economics, so even large productivity gains in preparation would not unlock proportional expansion in headcount. The occupation therefore remains resilient: AI may refine preparation and strategy but leaves the essential human physical role intact and does not drive net job loss or wholesale skill restructuring.

title: Athletic trainers
rationale: Core duties—on-field injury evaluation, emergency care, taping/bracing, and hands-on rehabilitation—require physical presence, manual skill, and real-time judgment in unpredictable sports environments, so AI only assists peripheral tasks like record-keeping, data-driven prevention plans, or diagnostic support from wearables/video. Demand elasticity is moderate because lower costs could expand coverage to more youth/amateur programs and active older adults, yet total volume remains constrained by the fixed number of sports participants and events rather than unlocking unlimited new consumption. With disruption only moderate, AI reshapes support tools without altering the occupation’s essential human-presence core, placing it firmly in the resilient category.

title: Atmospheric scientists, including meteorologists
rationale: Core work centers on computational modeling, data analysis, programming, forecast generation, and graphics—predominantly knowledge tasks where AI weather models (e.g., GraphCast-style systems) already deliver material speed and accuracy gains and will deepen further, driving high disruption even as physical instruments, severe-weather judgment, and public communication retain human elements. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper specialized forecasts unlock more private-sector use in energy, logistics, agriculture, and insurance, yet overall demand remains constrained by federal funding dependence, saturated free public forecasts, and limited need for 10x more baseline weather products. The combination produces restructuring: the occupation persists but shifts toward AI-oversight, interpretation, and domain-specific application skills.

title: Audiologists
rationale: Audiologists' core duties center on in-person patient exams, hands-on hearing-aid fitting, balance exercises, and counseling, which require physical presence and interpersonal skills; AI can assist with audiogram analysis, treatment planning, and record-keeping but does not displace the clinical interaction, yielding moderate disruption. Elasticity is moderate-to-high because untreated hearing loss is widespread, especially among aging adults and in access-constrained settings, so lower cost and faster throughput would expand screening, fittings, and follow-up care. With disruption only at the moderate level, AI mainly augments peripheral cognitive tasks while the occupation's patient-facing core remains intact, fitting the resilient category.

title: Automotive body and glass repairers
rationale: Core tasks center on physical, hands-on work—removing and welding parts, realigning frames, hammering dents, sanding, installing glass, and using pneumatic/hydraulic tools in shops or on-site—which AI cannot perform and which require human presence, dexterity, and strength; AI only peripherally aids damage estimates, photo-based assessment, or planning. Demand is driven by the fixed volume of collisions and vehicle damage rather than price, so even large productivity gains would not unlock substantially more repairs (safety tech is already reducing accidents); cheaper work might shift a few total-loss decisions or minor cosmetic fixes but remains structurally capped. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation stays resilient as AI does not reshape the core work.

title: Automotive service technicians and mechanics
rationale: Core work remains predominantly physical—lifting, disassembling, replacing mechanical and electronic parts with hand and power tools in a shop environment—while AI primarily augments the already-computerized diagnostic and documentation portions rather than replacing hands-on repair. Demand for repairs is largely fixed by the size of the vehicle fleet, usage patterns, and breakdown rates; even large cost or speed gains unlock only modest extra volume (e.g., more preventive work or delayed scrappage) rather than order-of-magnitude expansion. Because disruption stays moderate, the occupation is resilient: AI tools will raise productivity at the margin but will not reshape the essential on-site, physical nature of the job.

title: Bakers
rationale: Core baker duties—measuring and mixing ingredients, kneading and shaping dough, loading ovens, and monitoring physical baking—are overwhelmingly manual and require real-world presence around hot equipment and perishable materials; AI can only touch peripheral elements such as recipe scaling, demand forecasting, or vision-based quality checks. Demand for breads and pastries is largely fixed by population, dietary habits, and stomach capacity, so even large productivity gains would not unlock dramatically higher total consumption. Because disruption remains low, the occupation is resilient: AI may improve efficiency at the margins without reshaping the essential hands-on work.

title: Barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists
rationale: Core tasks—cutting, coloring, styling, shampooing, and client consultation—are almost entirely physical, manual, and require real-time human presence and dexterity with tools, so AI only touches peripheral elements such as style-recommendation apps, booking, payments, and inventory. Demand is constrained by hair-growth cycles, population size, and preference for in-person service; even large productivity gains would not unlock dramatically higher volume of haircuts or treatments. With disruption well below the threshold for structural change, the occupation remains resilient.

title: Bartenders
rationale: Core bartender tasks—physically mixing and pouring drinks, checking IDs, monitoring intoxication, cleaning, restocking, and real-time customer engagement—are overwhelmingly physical, sensory, and presence-based; AI currently assists only peripheral elements such as recipe lookup or inventory tracking and is not close to replacing the hands-on service loop. Demand elasticity is low because alcohol service and bar experiences face structural caps from social norms, health concerns, licensing rules, and limited leisure hours; even large productivity gains would not unlock dramatically higher total consumption. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation remains resilient: AI may trim admin edges but leaves the essential work and headcount trajectory largely intact.

title: Bill and account collectors
rationale: Core work is almost entirely digital and language-based—skip tracing via databases, outbound calling, scripted negotiation, record updates, and compliance checks—all of which AI voice agents, LLMs, and automated dialers already perform or assist at scale, with rapid further gains expected. Demand for collection services is largely fixed by the stock of overdue debt rather than suppressed by cost; making collection 10x cheaper mainly lets firms process the same accounts with far fewer people, with only modest expansion into marginal small-balance debts. This combination of high task substitutability and low demand elasticity produces net headcount contraction, consistent with the BLS’s projected 10% decline.

title: Biochemists and biophysicists
rationale: Core work mixes wet-lab experiments with heavy cognitive tasks (literature synthesis, experimental design, data analysis, molecular modeling, grant/paper writing); AI already materially transforms the latter via tools like AlphaFold, automated bioinformatics, and generative writing, placing the occupation in the high-disruption range even though physical lab presence remains. Demand is highly elastic because R&D cost and speed currently suppress output in drug discovery, agriculture, biofuels, and environmental applications; 10x cheaper/faster research would unlock far more projects and products as aging populations and biotech markets expand. High disruption plus high elasticity therefore yields augmentation: each scientist produces dramatically more discoveries while total headcount holds or grows.

title: Bioengineers and biomedical engineers
rationale: Core work centers on cognitive tasks—device/software design, statistical modeling and simulation, data analysis, technical writing, and research synthesis—all of which AI already accelerates via generative design, automated simulation, literature review, and report drafting, even while physical prototyping, lab experiments, installation, and clinician collaboration retain human presence. Demand is highly elastic because development cost and speed currently suppress the volume of medical devices, implants, diagnostics, and biotech solutions; dramatically cheaper and faster engineering unlocks large latent markets driven by aging populations, personalized medicine, and underserved needs. High disruption paired with high elasticity therefore yields augmentation: each engineer produces far more output while total employment holds or grows with expanded innovation pipelines.

title: Biological technicians
rationale: Core duties center on hands-on lab work—sample preparation, equipment setup/maintenance, and conducting physical experiments—which require real-world presence and manual precision that AI cannot fully replace, though AI already assists data analysis, modeling, documentation, and report writing. This mixed profile yields moderate disruption. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper/faster technician output would expand biotech R&D, synthetic biology, and testing volumes in pharma and environmental applications, yet funding, lab infrastructure, and regulatory constraints limit unlimited growth. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation remains resilient overall as AI augments rather than reshapes the physical core.

title: Boilermakers
rationale: Core boilermaker work is almost entirely physical and on-site—welding, aligning heavy plates, working inside confined vessels or at heights with hand/power tools—so AI has negligible impact beyond peripheral blueprint interpretation or planning aids; robotic welders already exist but do not remove the need for human presence in unpredictable industrial environments. Demand is largely inelastic because boiler and pressure-vessel needs are driven by industrial capacity, energy-plant type, and long asset lives rather than labor cost; the ongoing shift away from coal further caps any expansion. With disruption well below the threshold for material change, the occupation remains resilient regardless of modest elasticity.

title: Bookkeeping, accounting, and auditing clerks
rationale: Core tasks—transaction posting, classification, reconciliation, accuracy checks, and report generation—are almost entirely digital and cognitive, already heavily automated by accounting software and rapidly advancing AI tools for OCR, categorization, and anomaly detection, placing the occupation firmly in AI’s path. Demand for bookkeeping services is largely fixed by the volume of economic transactions and number of organizations; making the work 10x cheaper primarily reduces headcount rather than unlocking large new volumes of record-keeping, as confirmed by BLS projections of employment decline from automation. This combination of very high disruption and low elasticity produces net replacement, with significant contraction expected as AI absorbs routine processing.

title: Broadcast, sound, and video technicians
rationale: Core work mixes physical on-site tasks (equipment setup/takedown, cabling, installation, live adjustments, repairs, and heavy lifting at venues or towers) that require human presence and manual dexterity with digital/cognitive ones (software editing, signal monitoring, synchronization, and automated controls) that AI already assists via tools for mixing, noise reduction, and lighting cues; this yields moderate disruption as AI changes knowledge portions without eliminating the hands-on core. Elasticity is moderate because dramatically cheaper/faster AV services would unlock more corporate video, digital signage, podcasts, indie productions, and event setups, yet expansion is capped by finite live venues, broadcast slots, and audience capacity rather than unlimited latent demand. With disruption only moderate, the occupation remains resilient as AI primarily augments peripheral and software tasks while physical presence stays essential.

title: Budget analysts
rationale: Budget analysts perform predominantly digital knowledge work—consolidating data, running cost-benefit analyses, generating reports, forecasting needs, and monitoring compliance—that AI already handles well via financial models, generative tools, and automated dashboards, placing nearly all core tasks in AI’s direct path. Demand is low-elasticity because every organization needs a fixed annual budget process rather than unbounded additional analysis; cheaper/faster work does not unlock 10x more budgets or programs, especially given government funding and structural constraints that dominate employment. High disruption combined with limited demand expansion therefore points to net replacement and headcount contraction.

title: Bus drivers
rationale: Bus driving centers on physical vehicle operation, real-time traffic navigation, passenger assistance (including disabilities and school discipline), and safety enforcement in unpredictable environments, so AI only touches peripheral elements like GPS routing, predictive maintenance, or fare systems. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate because school bus needs are largely fixed by enrollment while transit/intercity ridership can expand somewhat with lower costs, yet remains constrained by infrastructure, public funding, and substitution with other modes. Disruption stays well below the threshold that would reshape core work, placing the occupation firmly in the resilient category regardless of modest demand responses.

title: Butchers
rationale: Core butcher work is overwhelmingly physical and manual—knife work, deboning, grinding, lifting carcasses, sanitation in cold rooms, and custom customer cuts—requiring real-world dexterity and presence that current and near-term AI cannot replace; AI only touches peripheral tasks like inventory tracking or sales forecasting. Demand for meat cutting is largely fixed by population-level consumption patterns and retail volume rather than price or speed of the cutting process itself, so productivity gains would shrink headcount rather than expand total output. Because disruption remains low, the occupation is resilient: AI does not reshape the essential hands-on role even if some admin efficiencies appear.

title: Calibration technologists and technicians
rationale: Core duties center on physical inspection, manual adjustment, testing, and preventive maintenance of real-world gauges, meters, and instruments in plants or labs, requiring dexterity, strength, and on-site presence that AI cannot perform; AI only assists peripheral tasks such as data logging, standards comparison, scheduling, and predictive analytics. Demand is largely fixed by the installed base of measurement devices plus regulatory and quality requirements, so even large productivity gains from AI or self-calibrating systems produce only modest expansion (slightly more frequent checks or broader adoption) rather than unlocking large latent volume. Because disruption remains moderate and well below the high-disruption threshold, the occupation is resilient: AI improves efficiency at the margins without reshaping the hands-on core or driving major headcount contraction.

title: Cardiovascular technologists and technicians
rationale: Core work centers on physical patient preparation/positioning, real-time operation of specialized hardware (cath labs, EKG machines, spirometers), and hands-on assistance during invasive procedures, so AI mainly augments the secondary analysis/summary/record-keeping steps rather than replacing the presence-dependent majority of tasks. Demand for cardiac and pulmonary testing is driven by disease prevalence and aging demographics and is constrained by physician orders, clinical guidelines, and facility capacity; cheaper/faster throughput unlocks only limited additional screening volume rather than order-of-magnitude expansion. Because disruption remains moderate, the occupation stays resilient overall.

title: Career and technical education teachers
rationale: Core duties center on in-person demonstration, supervision of tools/equipment, and hands-on labs (auto repair, welding, culinary, cosmetology), which require physical presence and real-time safety oversight that AI cannot replace; AI mainly assists peripheral knowledge tasks such as lesson planning, theory content generation, and some grading. Demand is constrained by fixed student demographics, school budgets, class-size norms, and regulatory structures, so productivity gains from AI tools are unlikely to unlock large expansions in total CTE teacher headcount. Because disruption remains only moderate, the occupation stays resilient overall even as AI reshapes prep work.

title: Carpenters
rationale: Core carpenter tasks—measuring, cutting, shaping, and installing wood and other materials on-site with hand and power tools—are overwhelmingly physical and require real-world presence, dexterity, and adaptation to variable conditions, so AI only touches peripheral planning, blueprint interpretation, or calculations. Demand for carpentry is somewhat elastic because lower costs could unlock more housing and renovation activity amid shortages, yet it remains constrained by land, materials, regulations, capital, and complementary trades. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation stays resilient: AI does not reshape the core work even if productivity edges higher.

title: Cartographers and photogrammetrists
rationale: Core tasks center on digital analysis of satellite/LiDAR imagery, GIS data integration, feature extraction, and map design/visualization—all highly amenable to computer vision, generative AI, and automated geospatial tools already in use today, with only secondary fieldwork. Demand is elastic because dramatically cheaper and faster mapping unlocks substantial latent uses in urban planning, environmental monitoring, disaster response, logistics, precision agriculture, real-time navigation, and commercial applications that were previously cost-prohibitive. High disruption combined with high elasticity means AI multiplies output per worker while expanding total volume of maps and analyses produced, supporting stable or growing headcount for those who adapt to AI-augmented workflows.

title: Cashiers
rationale: Core cashier duties—scanning items, processing payments, verifying ages, and handling returns—are already heavily automated via self-checkout systems, computer vision, and AI-enhanced POS tools, with further gains expected as these systems improve reliability and reduce human oversight needs; remaining physical tasks like bagging or light stocking are secondary and also shrinking. Demand for human checkout labor is highly inelastic because retail transaction volume does not expand proportionally with cheaper/faster processing—online sales and self-service simply reduce the number of human-handled transactions rather than unlocking latent demand for more cashiers. This combination of high task automation and fixed demand produces clear headcount contraction, matching the replace category and aligning with the projected 10% employment decline.

title: Chefs and head cooks
rationale: Core duties center on physical kitchen presence—tasting/smelling ingredients, hands-on cooking with knives and equipment, real-time supervision of staff, sanitation, and quality control in a fast-paced environment—while AI only assists peripheral cognitive tasks such as recipe ideation, menu optimization, inventory software, and admin. Demand for dining experiences and high-quality prepared food can expand moderately if AI lowers costs and improves consistency (more restaurants, catering, and healthier options), but is constrained by physical limits on meal consumption and dining frequency rather than being heavily suppressed. Because disruption remains moderate, the occupation is resilient: AI augments edges without reshaping the essential human role.

title: Chemical engineers
rationale: Core work is predominantly knowledge-based—process modeling, equipment design via CAD, research, cost estimation, optimization, and regulatory analysis—all of which AI already accelerates through simulation, generative design, and data-driven process control, even though plant visits and safety judgment still require human presence. Elasticity is moderate because dramatically cheaper process engineering unlocks more R&D in sustainability, biotech, nanomaterials, and specialty chemicals, yet physical capital intensity, plant construction timelines, and regulation prevent unlimited expansion of demand. High disruption paired with only moderate demand growth means the occupation persists but shifts heavily toward AI-fluent oversight, creative problem-solving, and interdisciplinary work; non-adapters face displacement.

title: Chemical technicians
rationale: Disruption is moderate because core duties center on physical lab presence—preparing solutions, setting up and maintaining instruments, handling chemicals, and troubleshooting equipment—while AI mainly accelerates the secondary cognitive pieces of data interpretation, process monitoring, and report generation. Elasticity is also moderate: cheaper, faster analysis and experimentation would unlock some additional R&D, materials testing, and quality-control volume (especially around sustainability and new products), yet overall demand remains tethered to chemical manufacturing output and regulatory requirements rather than expanding unboundedly. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is classified resilient; AI will change peripheral workflows but will not fundamentally reshape the hands-on technician role.

title: Chemists and materials scientists
rationale: Core work mixes physical lab procedures with heavy cognitive tasks—research planning, molecular modeling/simulation, data analysis, property prediction, and technical reporting—where AI tools (generative chemistry models, automated experiment design, literature synthesis) already materially accelerate and reshape daily practice, placing disruption in the high range. Demand elasticity is high because R&D cost and speed currently constrain the volume of materials, drugs, batteries, and specialty chemicals pursued; 10x cheaper/faster discovery unlocks substantial latent commercial and societal demand for new products across energy, health, electronics, and sustainability. The combination produces an augment outcome: each chemist/materials scientist becomes far more productive while total output and headcount expand rather than contract.

title: Childcare workers
rationale: Core duties—physical supervision, diapering, feeding, hygiene, real-time safety monitoring, and in-person play/emotional care—require unpredictable human presence and cannot be automated by AI in any meaningful way over the next decade; AI only assists peripheral tasks such as activity planning, curriculum ideas, and record-keeping. Demand elasticity is moderate because high current costs suppress some formal childcare use and cheaper provision could raise labor-force participation and hours demanded, yet total volume remains constrained by birth rates, regulated staff-to-child ratios, and parental preferences for human caregivers. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation remains resilient: AI touches the edges without reshaping the job or displacing workers at scale.

title: Chiropractors
rationale: Core work centers on hands-on physical examination, spinal/joint manipulation, and in-person neuromusculoskeletal therapy that require dexterity, patient presence, and real-time tactile feedback; AI can assist only peripheral elements such as history review, imaging interpretation, lifestyle advice, and practice admin, keeping disruption moderate. Demand elasticity is moderate because lower cost or higher throughput could expand access for back/neck pain and wellness care among aging populations and those currently deterred by price or limited insurance, yet total volume remains bounded by clinical need rather than unlimited latent demand. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation stays resilient: AI tools may improve efficiency and diagnostics at the margins without reshaping the essential human-delivered physical care.

title: Civil engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: Core tasks mix heavily AI-vulnerable digital work (CAD drafting, plan review, cost estimation, report writing, data analysis) with essential physical presence for field surveys, material/soil testing, and site inspections, so AI already assists and will reshape the knowledge portions substantially while leaving hands-on elements intact. Demand elasticity is low because infrastructure volume is constrained by government budgets, physical needs, regulation, and the fact that design/tech labor is only a fraction of total project cost; cheaper/faster technician output therefore unlocks only modest additional projects rather than large latent demand. With disruption at the upper end of moderate/high but still ≤6, the occupation remains resilient overall as AI augments peripheral and office tasks without eliminating the need for on-site human roles.

title: Civil engineers
rationale: Disruption is high because core tasks—CAD/BIM design, structural and hydraulic analysis, cost estimation, code compliance checks, and report generation—are predominantly digital/cognitive and already being accelerated by generative design, simulation, and AI review tools, even though site supervision, PE sign-off, and stakeholder coordination still require human presence. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster engineering unlocks more infrastructure projects, climate-resilience upgrades, and private development that are currently cost-constrained, yet overall volume remains capped by public budgets, construction labor/materials bottlenecks, and regulatory timelines. The combination produces restructure: the occupation persists and may even grow modestly, but the skill mix shifts heavily toward AI orchestration, judgment, and field oversight, displacing those who cannot adapt.

title: Claims adjusters, appraisers, examiners, and investigators
rationale: Core work is predominantly cognitive—document review, coverage determination, cost estimation from photos/data, fraud pattern detection, and settlement negotiation—already being materially automated by image-analysis software, AI claim estimators, and predictive models, even though some on-site inspections and surveillance remain. Demand volume is driven by real-world insured events (accidents, disasters, medical incidents) rather than processing cost or speed, so productivity gains translate mostly into fewer workers rather than more claims handled. This combination of high disruption and low elasticity produces net headcount contraction, consistent with the BLS projection of decline.

title: Clinical laboratory technologists and technicians
rationale: Core duties center on physical specimen handling, equipment operation/calibration, slide preparation, and biohazard protocols that require on-site human presence and dexterity, while AI already assists image analysis (cytology/hematology), result interpretation, and data entry—producing moderate rather than transformative change. Demand for laboratory tests is largely fixed by physician orders, clinical guidelines, insurance rules, and population health needs; cheaper/faster processing unlocks only limited extra screening or genetic testing rather than open-ended volume growth. Because disruption stays at or below the moderate threshold, the occupation remains resilient: AI raises productivity and may slow headcount growth (as BLS already notes) but does not eliminate the need for skilled technologists and technicians.

title: Coaches and scouts
rationale: Core coaching duties center on in-person practice leadership, real-time game decisions, athlete motivation, technique demonstration, and relationship-based recruiting, all of which require physical presence and interpersonal judgment that AI cannot replace; AI already assists peripheral analytical tasks such as video performance review, opponent scouting data, and conditioning plan optimization, producing moderate overall disruption. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper, higher-quality analysis and planning can expand private instruction, youth programs, and recreational sports somewhat, yet the bulk of positions remain anchored to fixed numbers of school teams, college programs, and professional rosters. The combination of only moderate disruption with limited demand expansion places the occupation firmly in the resilient category.

title: Community health workers
rationale: Disruption is moderate because core duties center on in-person outreach, home visits, trust-building, cultural mediation, and interpersonal coaching/advocacy that require physical presence and lived community ties; AI can only assist peripheral tasks such as generating educational materials, translation, data tracking, and case documentation. Elasticity is moderate because substantial unmet need exists in underserved populations for preventive care navigation and social-determinant support, so productivity tools could expand program reach, yet growth remains constrained by public funding, grants, and the irreplaceable human-contact component. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI augments administrative and informational edges without reshaping the field-based human core.

title: Compensation and benefits managers
rationale: Core duties center on data analysis of wages/benefits, market benchmarking, regulatory compliance, plan design, budgeting, and recommendations—predominantly digital knowledge work where AI already accelerates research, modeling, reporting, and optimization, with trajectory toward handling most analytical and drafting tasks. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper/faster design unlocks more sophisticated or frequent compensation reviews (especially for mid-size firms and pay-equity/wellness programs) yet overall demand remains constrained by the fixed number of organizations needing the function and ongoing outsourcing of admin elements. High disruption plus moderate elasticity means the role survives via substantial skill shift toward AI oversight, vendor strategy, and executive judgment, displacing those who remain pure analysts.

title: Compensation, benefits, and job analysis specialists
rationale: Core duties—market research, data/cost analysis of pay and benefits, job description evaluation, compliance checks, and report generation—are almost entirely digital/cognitive knowledge work already materially assisted by AI analytics, benchmarking tools, and generative drafting, placing the occupation firmly in the high-disruption range. Elasticity is only moderate because cheaper/faster analysis unlocks some latent demand (more frequent equity reviews, customized packages for mid-size firms, continuous rather than annual benchmarking), yet total volume remains capped by the finite number of employers and regulatory cadence rather than expanding unboundedly. High disruption plus moderate elasticity therefore produces restructuring: pure analytical headcount contracts while remaining roles shift toward AI oversight, strategic judgment, and stakeholder presentation.

title: Compliance officers
rationale: Core tasks—researching and interpreting regulations, drafting policies, risk assessment, document-based audits, report writing, and training material creation—are predominantly cognitive and language-based, already being reshaped by RegTech and LLMs that monitor rules, flag issues, and generate drafts. Physical inspections and stakeholder interviews remain human but are secondary for most roles. Demand expands moderately because cheaper, faster compliance unlocks more thorough programs, continuous monitoring, and adoption by smaller firms or new regulatory domains, yet overall volume is still anchored to mandatory legal requirements rather than unlimited latent consumption. High disruption plus moderate elasticity therefore shifts the skill mix toward AI oversight and data-driven judgment without eliminating the occupation or producing explosive headcount growth.

title: Computer and information research scientists
rationale: Core tasks—algorithm design, coding new systems, experimental analysis with ML/data science, theory development, and paper writing—are almost entirely digital and cognitive, already heavily assisted by AI coding agents, hypothesis generators, and literature tools, placing the occupation squarely in AI’s path. Demand elasticity is high because dramatically cheaper and faster research unlocks latent demand for more innovation across AI itself, cybersecurity, robotics, and data-intensive domains; society and firms will fund far more R&D when the cost of exploration drops. The combination produces an augment outcome: each scientist becomes far more productive while total research output and headcount expand rather than contract.

title: Computer and information systems managers
rationale: Core duties such as analyzing IT needs, cost-benefit assessment, security process design, and project planning are predominantly cognitive and digital, so AI tools already provide material assistance in analysis, threat detection, and recommendation generation and will reshape daily workflows further. Leadership of staff, executive communication, vendor negotiation, and high-stakes resource allocation still require human judgment and presence, keeping disruption in the high rather than maximum range. Demand elasticity is high because organizations’ expanding reliance on cloud, cybersecurity, digital platforms, and AI itself creates substantial latent need for IT strategy and oversight; productivity gains therefore translate into more systems managed and more firms adopting sophisticated IT rather than pure headcount reduction, consistent with the projected 15% employment growth.

title: Computer hardware engineers
rationale: Core work centers on digital design, simulation, schematic creation, test analysis, and optimization of processors and circuits—tasks already materially accelerated by AI-driven EDA tools, generative placement/routing, and verification—while physical prototyping and manufacturing oversight remain secondary. Demand elasticity is high because the extreme cost and time of custom silicon currently suppress innovation; 10x cheaper/faster design unlocks far more specialized chips, edge devices, automotive systems, and IoT hardware that were previously uneconomical. The combination of high disruption and high elasticity means each engineer produces dramatically more designs, expanding total output and supporting stable or growing headcount rather than contraction.

title: Computer network architects
rationale: Core work centers on cognitive tasks—network topology design, performance analysis, security planning, documentation, and technology research—which AI already accelerates via simulation, config generation, traffic optimization, and AIOps tools, even as occasional hardware deployment and org-specific integration retain a human element, yielding high disruption. Elasticity is high because dramatically cheaper/faster design removes cost barriers that currently suppress upgrades, cloud migrations, edge/IoT builds, and AI-ready infrastructure across firms of all sizes. The combination produces an augment outcome: each architect handles far more complex or numerous projects while overall demand for robust networks expands with digital transformation, supporting stable-to-growing headcount rather than contraction.

title: Computer programmers
rationale: Writing, modifying, testing, and debugging code is almost entirely digital/cognitive work already being materially accelerated by AI coding assistants, with rapid further trajectory toward automation of core tasks. Cheaper/faster programming unlocks meaningful latent demand for more software, features, and custom applications, yet expansion is only moderate because many tasks shift upward to software developers or get fully automated, constraining pure programmer headcount. High disruption plus mid-range elasticity therefore produces restructure: the occupation persists but requires substantial adaptation to AI-augmented workflows.

title: Computer support specialists
rationale: Core tasks of diagnosing user-described problems, guiding step-by-step fixes, documenting tickets, and routine network monitoring are almost entirely digital/language-based and already being handled by AI chatbots and automated tools, with BLS explicitly citing this automation as a driver of decline; physical setup/repair is a minority of the work. Demand for support services expands only modestly with cheaper delivery (more small firms or devices covered) but is fundamentally capped by the volume of actual problems and systems rather than unlocking near-unlimited new consumption. High disruption plus low elasticity therefore produces net headcount contraction as AI absorbs the bulk of routine tickets without commensurate growth in total work.

title: Computer systems analysts
rationale: Core tasks—requirements analysis, systems design, cost-benefit modeling, data modeling, documentation, testing, and light programming—are almost entirely digital/cognitive and already materially accelerated by AI coding assistants, architecture generators, and analytics tools, producing very high disruption. Elasticity is high because cheaper, faster systems work unlocks latent demand: more frequent upgrades, deeper customization, continuous optimization, and AI-system integration projects that smaller firms previously deferred. The result is an augment dynamic in which each analyst produces far more value and overall employment holds or expands as organizations consume more systems-improvement work.

title: Concierges
rationale: Disruption is moderate because roughly half the duties (recommendations, reservations, tickets, info, emails) are language/cognitive and already assisted by AI apps and chatbots, while the other half (greeting, packages, errands, in-person problem-solving, relationship-building) requires physical presence and unpredictable real-world interaction that AI cannot replace. Elasticity is low because demand is largely tied to the fixed stock of hotels, apartments, and offices that choose to staff a desk; cheaper service unlocks some additional residential/senior facilities but does not create dramatically higher volume of human concierge work. The combination keeps the occupation in the resilient category: AI trims peripheral tasks and accelerates hotel automation already noted by BLS, yet core human-facing work remains intact.

title: Conservation scientists and foresters
rationale: Core work mixes substantial outdoor physical tasks (site preparation with equipment, fire suppression, on-site tree measurement with clinometers and tapes, long-distance terrain walking) with knowledge work (GIS/satellite analysis, management planning, compliance, landowner negotiation), so AI will strongly assist data modeling, remote sensing interpretation, and plan optimization but cannot replace required real-world presence. Demand is constrained by finite public and private land acreage, government budgets, and regulatory structures; cheaper analysis may modestly expand private-landowner advisory work or wildfire mitigation intensity but will not unlock large latent volume. Because disruption remains moderate, the occupation is resilient—AI reshapes analytical tools without displacing the hands-on core.

title: Construction and building inspectors
rationale: Core work mixes on-site physical inspection (climbing, crawling, using meters/testers, verifying systems and structures in unpredictable real-world conditions) with knowledge tasks like plan review, code checking, and report writing; AI already assists the latter via blueprint analysis, image processing, report generation, and remote/drone inspections, but human presence and judgment remain essential for most site work, keeping disruption moderate. Demand is largely fixed by construction volume, permitting rules, and safety regulations rather than price or speed, so cheaper/faster inspections unlock only limited extra volume (e.g., more home checks) and do not expand total need enough to offset productivity gains. Because disruption stays at or below the moderate threshold, the occupation is resilient overall even as tools restructure peripheral tasks.

title: Construction equipment operators
rationale: Core tasks are almost entirely physical and site-based—maneuvering heavy machinery via levers/pedals, coordinating with crews via signals, and performing basic maintenance in unpredictable outdoor environments—so AI currently affects only peripherals like GPS precision aids, predictive maintenance, or training simulators, keeping disruption low. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper/faster equipment operation would unlock some additional infrastructure and building projects currently delayed by cost, yet demand remains constrained by materials, capital budgets, regulations, and physical site limits rather than expanding unboundedly. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation stays resilient as AI does not reshape the essential human presence and control required on construction sites.

title: Construction laborers and helpers
rationale: Core tasks—site cleanup, material handling, trench digging, scaffolding, and power-tool operation—are almost entirely physical, outdoor, and presence-dependent, so AI affects only peripheral planning or safety monitoring rather than the work itself. Demand is moderately elastic because lower effective labor costs would unlock additional housing, renovation, and infrastructure projects that are currently constrained by expense. With disruption well below the threshold that reshapes the occupation, the net effect is resilient: AI remains a minor adjunct while headcount continues to track overall construction volume.

title: Construction managers
rationale: Core duties center on onsite supervision, real-time response to delays/emergencies, subcontractor coordination, and physical-site decision-making that require human presence and judgment, so AI mainly accelerates peripheral knowledge tasks such as cost estimating, scheduling, contract review, and progress reporting rather than replacing the occupation’s essence. Demand for construction management is driven by population growth, infrastructure needs, and building complexity rather than management cost alone; even large productivity gains are unlikely to unlock dramatically more projects because capital, materials, land, and trade labor remain the binding constraints. With only moderate disruption, the occupation fits the resilient category: AI tools will raise individual productivity but leave the fundamental role and headcount trajectory largely intact.

title: Cooks
rationale: Core duties such as weighing ingredients, grilling/frying/boiling, plating, and maintaining sanitation are almost entirely physical, manual, and sensory, requiring on-site presence and dexterity that current and near-term AI cannot replace; AI only assists peripheral tasks like inventory forecasting or recipe suggestions. Demand elasticity is moderate because substantially cheaper/faster food preparation would expand restaurant openings, takeout/delivery volume, institutional catering, and personal-chef services as price barriers fall, though biological limits on consumption and kitchen capacity prevent unbounded growth. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation stays resilient: AI touches the edges without reshaping the hands-on core.

title: Correctional officers and bailiffs
rationale: Core duties—physical supervision, cell searches, restraint, escorting inmates, and maintaining order in volatile environments—require real-world human presence, strength, and split-second judgment that AI cannot perform; AI only assists peripheral tasks such as camera analytics, automated logs, and risk scoring. Demand for correctional capacity is set by crime rates, sentencing laws, and budgets rather than labor cost or speed, so cheaper AI-augmented monitoring does not expand the number of prisoners or courtrooms and may even reduce staffing needs. Because disruption remains low, the occupation stays resilient even as technology improves surveillance efficiency.

title: Cost estimators
rationale: Core tasks—reading blueprints and technical documents, querying cost databases, calculating material/labor/time estimates, running simulations, and producing bids/reports—are almost entirely digital and cognitive, already being accelerated by estimation software and highly amenable to multimodal AI and predictive models. Demand for estimates is tightly coupled to the volume of construction and manufacturing projects, which is set by broader economic activity rather than estimation cost; cheaper/faster estimates enable more iterations or slightly better coverage but do not unlock large latent project volume. High disruption plus low elasticity therefore points to net headcount contraction as productivity gains are not absorbed by expanded output.

title: Court reporters and simultaneous captioners
rationale: Core tasks center on real-time speech-to-text transcription, speaker identification, and producing verbatim legal or accessibility records—almost entirely language and digital work already being transformed by AI tools like advanced ASR systems that generate drafts for human review. Physical presence is declining with remote options, and accuracy/legal certification barriers are eroding as models improve on multi-speaker, technical, and noisy audio. Demand for official court transcripts is tightly constrained by the volume of legal proceedings, judicial budgets, and regulatory requirements rather than price, so cheaper output does not generate proportionally more cases or depositions; captioning sees only modest expansion from accessibility rules and demographics, most of which AI auto-captions already absorb. High disruption plus low elasticity therefore points to replace, with headcount contraction as AI handles the bulk of capture and humans shrink to residual editing/oversight roles.

title: Craft and fine artists
rationale: Core tasks for most craft and fine artists center on physical manipulation of materials (pottery, glassblowing, painting, sculpting, fiber work, jewelry) that require dexterity, real-world presence, and unpredictable material handling; AI assists ideation, digital sketching, portfolios, and marketing but leaves the hands-on creation largely intact, placing disruption in the moderate mixed range. Demand for original handmade or fine art is only modestly elastic—cheaper production unlocks some commercial illustration and decorative use but is constrained by collector preferences for authenticity, limited display space, and competition from machine-made substitutes, so productivity gains do not expand total headcount much. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation remains resilient overall, with AI touching periphery rather than reshaping the core craft.

title: Credit counselors
rationale: Core duties such as assessing client finances, calculating debt management plans and budgets, preparing documents, and explaining options are predominantly cognitive, language-based, and digital, so AI tools already automate analysis, optimization, drafting, and initial advice while human empathy remains relevant for interviews and negotiations. Elasticity is moderate because lower cost and higher speed can expand access for underserved individuals and small cases currently deterred by barriers, yet overall volume is still bounded by the finite population experiencing debt distress plus existing free nonprofit capacity. The combination produces restructure: AI will reshape required skills toward AI oversight, complex interpersonal cases, and specialized negotiation, so non-adapters face displacement while adapters remain viable.

title: Customer service representatives
rationale: Core tasks—listening to inquiries, providing product info, processing orders/returns, and resolving complaints—are almost entirely language-based, digital, and cognitive, already being handled at scale by AI chatbots, voice agents, and generative tools that continue to improve on complex cases. Demand elasticity is low because customer service is primarily a cost center whose volume is driven by existing customers and transactions rather than latent unmet need; making it 10x cheaper mainly reduces headcount instead of expanding total interactions. This combination of high disruption and limited demand expansion produces net replacement, consistent with the BLS projection of employment decline from automation and self-service.

title: Dancers and choreographers
rationale: Core dancer tasks center on physical athleticism, live rehearsal, and embodied performance that require real-world presence and cannot be automated, while choreographers' creative sequencing, music selection, and admin can be assisted by generative AI and motion tools yet still demand in-person demonstration, teaching, and artistic judgment with human bodies; this produces moderate disruption focused on knowledge portions. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster routine creation could expand digital content, social-media dance, and private studio instruction somewhat, but live performance demand is constrained by venue capacity, cultural interest, and arts funding rather than pure cost. With disruption well below the high threshold, AI touches the periphery without reshaping the occupation's physical core, so the net effect is resilient.

title: Data scientists
rationale: Data science consists almost entirely of digital cognitive work—coding, data cleaning, algorithm/model development, statistical analysis, visualization, and insight communication—all of which current generative AI, AutoML, and coding assistants already materially accelerate and partially automate. Demand elasticity is high because the high cost and scarcity of skilled practitioners currently suppress analytics adoption; 10x cheaper/faster output would unlock substantial latent demand for more models, personalized products, and data-driven decisions across firms of all sizes. The result is that productivity gains expand total work volume enough to keep headcount stable or growing, so AI augments rather than replaces the occupation.

title: Database administrators and architects
rationale: Core tasks—schema design, SQL coding, query optimization, security configuration, monitoring, and backups—are almost entirely digital and cognitive, already materially assisted by AI copilots, autonomous database features, and cloud automation tools, placing the occupation firmly in AI’s path. Elasticity is only moderate because exponential data growth and AI infrastructure needs expand demand for sophisticated architecture, yet cloud consolidation and self-managing systems simultaneously shrink the need for routine administration, so productivity gains are only partially absorbed by higher output. The net result is substantial skill-set shift toward architecture, AI oversight, and complex systems design rather than pure headcount growth or collapse; workers who fail to adapt face displacement while those who do remain essential.

title: Delivery truck drivers and driver/sales workers
rationale: Core tasks center on physical driving in complex urban environments, loading/unloading packages, and in-person customer handoffs or sales, all of which require real-world presence and remain far from full AI automation over a 10-year horizon; AI already aids peripheral elements like route optimization, paperwork, and dispatch apps but does not reshape the hands-on work. Demand elasticity is high because dramatically cheaper/faster delivery would unlock substantial latent e-commerce, food, grocery, and same-day service volume that is currently constrained by cost and speed. The occupation therefore stays resilient: AI touches the edges without displacing the physical core, while any productivity gains are absorbed by expanding delivery volume rather than headcount cuts.

title: Dental and ophthalmic laboratory technicians and medical appliance technicians
rationale: Core tasks remain heavily physical—bending, forming, polishing, and adjusting materials with hand and power tools—while digital elements (CAD software, 3D printing, work-order interpretation) are growing but still secondary; AI already assists generative design and visual inspection yet cannot replace the dexterity and real-world finishing required. Demand is largely fixed by clinical prescriptions, aging demographics, and medical necessity rather than price; cheaper/faster production may unlock modest upgrades or access for some patients but will not produce large volume expansion. Because disruption stays moderate, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes design and automation peripherally without eliminating the hands-on core.

title: Dental assistants
rationale: Core duties are predominantly physical and presence-based—chairside instrument handling, sterilization, suction, patient positioning, impressions, and x-ray capture—which AI cannot perform and which require dexterity and real-time human interaction; AI only touches peripheral admin (scheduling, records, billing) and limited image support. Demand for dental services has moderate elasticity because lower effective costs and higher practice throughput can unlock some latent preventive and restorative care among cost-sensitive or underserved patients, amplified by aging demographics, yet overall volume remains constrained by dentist supply, insurance, and clinical need rather than expanding unboundedly. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation remains resilient: AI augments office efficiency at the margins without reshaping the hands-on role.

title: Dental hygienists
rationale: Core tasks center on manual, in-mouth procedures requiring fine motor dexterity, physical tools, and real-time patient presence (tartar removal, polishing, sealants), so AI only peripherally assists with x-ray interpretation, charting, or education materials. Demand has some price sensitivity and latent access gaps that cheaper services could partially unlock, yet is constrained by fixed clinical frequency (e.g., twice-yearly cleanings), chair time, and regulatory scope-of-practice limits, preventing large expansion. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation remains resilient as AI does not reshape the essential hands-on work.

title: Dentists
rationale: Core dental work remains predominantly physical and manual—drilling, extractions, restorations, and chairside procedures requiring dexterity, tactile feedback, and real-time patient presence—so AI currently assists only knowledge portions such as x-ray interpretation, treatment planning, and digital scanning rather than replacing the hands-on tasks. Demand elasticity is moderate because lower costs and faster workflows would unlock some latent volume in cosmetics, preventive care, and underserved populations, yet overall need is still bounded by population oral-health incidence and insurance structures rather than expanding unboundedly. With disruption only moderate, the occupation stays resilient: AI reshapes diagnostics and admin but leaves the essential clinical skill set intact.

title: Desktop publishers
rationale: Core tasks—importing and integrating text/graphics, adjusting layouts, editing images, and preparing final files—are almost entirely digital and already heavily assisted by generative AI design tools (Adobe Firefly, Canva Magic Design, layout generators), placing the occupation squarely in AI’s path with rapid further automation expected. Demand elasticity is low because the volume of professional page-layout work is constrained by shrinking print media and the fact that cheaper tools simply shift production to non-specialists or end-users rather than expanding the market for dedicated desktop publishers.
