BLS already projects a 12% decline as tasks migrate to graphic designers, editors, and self-service platforms; AI accelerates that substitution without unlocking offsetting new demand. High disruption combined with inelastic demand therefore produces net replacement and headcount contraction.

title: Diagnostic medical sonographers
rationale: Core work centers on real-time physical probe manipulation, patient positioning, and hand-eye coordination in response to live anatomy, which AI cannot fully automate within 10 years; AI mainly assists the secondary image-review and measurement tasks, placing disruption in the moderate mixed range. Demand for ultrasound services has meaningful elasticity because lower cost and higher throughput expand point-of-care use, screening frequency, and specialty applications beyond current capacity constraints, though medical necessity and ordering protocols prevent unlimited growth. With disruption remaining at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI augments efficiency and quality at the margins without reshaping the hands-on core.

title: Diesel service technicians and mechanics
rationale: Core work centers on physical inspection, disassembly, repair, and reassembly of heavy diesel engines, brakes, and components using hand and power tools, plus test-driving—tasks that require on-site presence, strength, and dexterity that AI cannot perform. AI already aids the growing electronic diagnostics and manual interpretation portions and will improve predictive maintenance, but these remain secondary to hands-on repair, keeping disruption moderate. Demand for diesel repairs is largely fixed by the size and utilization of the truck/bus fleet rather than price or speed; cheaper/faster service unlocks little latent volume, so productivity gains mainly reduce headcount needs. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation remains resilient overall.

title: Dietitians and nutritionists
rationale: AI already assists core knowledge tasks such as generating personalized meal plans from client data and preferences, synthesizing nutrition research, creating educational materials, and automating documentation, making tools materially useful today and raising disruption into the high range. However, client counseling, empathetic assessment of health needs and behaviors, clinical collaboration, and in-person or regulated medical nutrition therapy still require human presence and judgment, preventing higher scores. Demand elasticity is moderate because lower cost and faster delivery would expand access to wellness, preventive, and corporate nutrition services for more individuals and organizations amid rising chronic disease and aging populations, yet healthcare regulations, insurance constraints, and fixed clinical caseloads limit unbounded growth. With disruption at the boundary of high but not exceeding the resilient threshold, AI primarily augments rather than displaces the occupation.

title: Drafters
rationale: Core drafting work is almost entirely digital—converting sketches and specs into CAD/BIM technical drawings, dimensions, and schematics—which places it squarely in AI’s path via generative design, text-to-CAD, and automated detailing tools already emerging today. Demand elasticity is low because the volume of technical drawings is tightly coupled to physical construction and manufacturing output, which is constrained by capital, materials, regulations, and real-world project pipelines rather than drafting cost; cheaper drafting unlocks some extra iterations or small-project access but does not produce 10x more buildings or machines. High disruption combined with limited demand expansion means AI and upstream engineers/architects absorb the work, producing net headcount contraction consistent with the already-flat BLS outlook under earlier CAD/BIM productivity gains.

title: Drywall installers, ceiling tile installers, and tapers
rationale: Core tasks—measuring/cutting/hanging heavy panels, working on stilts or scaffolds, taping joints, and sanding—are almost entirely physical, manual, and site-specific, so AI tools affect only peripheral planning or estimating and leave the occupation largely unchanged over the next decade. Demand is driven by the volume of new construction and remodeling rather than the unit cost of drywall labor; even large productivity gains would not unlock dramatically more buildings or renovations given capital, land, and regulatory constraints. Because disruption remains low, the occupation is resilient: AI does not reshape daily work or produce large headcount shifts.

title: Economists
rationale: Economists' core work—data collection and statistical analysis, mathematical modeling, forecasting, report writing, and research synthesis—is almost entirely digital and cognitive, placing it squarely in AI's path; current tools already accelerate coding, literature review, and draft generation, with rapid further gains expected. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster analysis will expand private-sector consulting, business forecasting, and specialized research, yet a large share of positions sit in government agencies whose headcount is budget-constrained and does not scale freely with productivity. High disruption combined with only moderate demand expansion therefore restructures the occupation: routine modeling and drafting shrink while interpretive judgment, policy advising, and AI orchestration grow, requiring substantial skill shifts for workers to remain competitive.

title: Editors
rationale: Editors' core work—grammar/style correction, rewriting for clarity, fact verification, content evaluation, and layout decisions—is almost entirely digital language and cognitive labor already heavily assisted by AI tools, placing nearly all daily tasks in AI's direct path and driving a very high disruption score. Elasticity is only moderate because cheaper/faster editing would unlock some latent demand (more self-published books, corporate content, and digital media polished to professional standards), yet structural limits from media consolidation, declining print, and the rise of unedited or fully AI-generated content prevent dramatic volume expansion. High disruption paired with moderate elasticity means the occupation persists but restructures around AI oversight, high-level judgment, and writer collaboration; workers who fail to adapt face displacement.

title: Electrical and electronic engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: Core duties center on hands-on assembly of prototypes, physical calibration/repair of instruments and circuitry, use of machine tools, and on-site observation, which require human presence and mechanical skill; AI already aids diagram generation, test-data analysis, diagnostics, and report writing but leaves the physical majority of tasks largely intact, producing only moderate disruption. Elasticity is moderate because lower cost and faster technical support would unlock additional prototyping, quality testing, and maintenance across growing electronics, semiconductor, medical-device, and automation markets, yet physical production volumes, factory constraints, and existing automation cap unlimited expansion. With disruption well below the high threshold, AI remains peripheral and the occupation stays resilient.

title: Electrical and electronics engineers
rationale: Core work is predominantly knowledge-based—requirements definition, CAD/simulation modeling, circuit and system design, analysis, and documentation—where generative AI, optimization tools, and automated verification already materially accelerate tasks, even though physical testing, site visits, and manufacturing supervision retain a human presence component. Demand is highly elastic because cheaper, faster engineering unlocks far more product variants, custom systems, renewable-energy infrastructure, semiconductors, EVs, and communications gear that are currently constrained by design cost and cycle time. High disruption combined with high elasticity means each engineer produces dramatically more output while total employment holds or grows as latent demand expands.

title: Electrical and electronics installers and repairers
rationale: Core work is predominantly physical and on-site—disassembling equipment, using hand tools, lifting heavy components, and working in factories, vehicles, or powerhouses—so AI only assists peripheral tasks like software-aided diagnostics, signal interpretation, and record-keeping rather than reshaping the job. Demand is largely inelastic because the volume of installations and repairs is driven by the existing stock of industrial, transportation, and utility equipment rather than price or speed; cheaper diagnostics may slightly increase maintenance but will not unlock large latent demand. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation remains resilient as AI stays at the periphery.

title: Electrical power-line installers and repairers
rationale: Core tasks—climbing poles/towers, stringing high-voltage cables, operating heavy equipment outdoors in all weather, and hands-on repair of live lines—are almost entirely physical and site-specific, so AI only assists peripheral diagnostics, drone inspections, or scheduling rather than reshaping daily work. Demand for grid expansion, EV connections, and storm restoration has some room to grow if labor costs fell, but is still constrained by capital, permitting, materials, and overall electricity consumption growth rather than pure labor price. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate, the occupation stays resilient regardless of moderate elasticity.

title: Electricians
rationale: Core electrician work—installing, troubleshooting, and repairing physical wiring, fixtures, and systems on-site with hand/power tools—is overwhelmingly manual and location-bound, so AI only assists peripheral tasks like blueprint interpretation, diagnostics, code checks, or job estimating. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper/faster electrical work would unlock some additional retrofits, EV chargers, and solar integrations, yet total volume remains constrained by the physical stock of buildings and construction cycles rather than exploding. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation stays resilient: AI tools may raise individual productivity modestly without reshaping headcount or the essential skill set.

title: Electro-mechanical and mechatronics technologists and technicians
rationale: Core duties center on hands-on physical work—operating metalworking machines, soldering, calibrating hydraulics/pneumatics, inspecting parts with precision tools, and maintaining robotic equipment on-site—which require presence, dexterity, and mechanical skill that AI cannot fully replace within 10 years; AI mainly assists peripheral cognitive tasks such as interpreting schematics, analyzing test data, predictive diagnostics, and report writing. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster support for electromechanical and robotic systems would modestly unlock greater automation adoption in manufacturing, R&D, and unmanned applications, expanding the installed base of equipment that still needs human technicians, though capital intensity and industrial structure limit unbounded growth. With disruption only moderate, the occupation remains resilient: AI reshapes tools and efficiency at the margin without displacing the essential on-site role.

title: Elementary, middle, and high school principals
rationale: Core duties mix knowledge work (data analysis, budgets, curriculum, scheduling, reports) that AI already assists with interpersonal leadership requiring physical presence (teacher observation/evaluation, student discipline/counseling, parent meetings, staff management, security, community representation), placing disruption in the moderate range. Demand is structurally capped by student enrollment, number of schools, and district budgets rather than principal cost or speed, so productivity gains are unlikely to expand headcount and may even enable consolidation. This keeps the occupation resilient: AI augments peripheral admin but does not reshape the human-centered core of school leadership.

title: Elevator and escalator installers and repairers
rationale: Core tasks center on physical assembly, heavy lifting, wiring, and on-site repair inside shafts and machine rooms using tools and hoists, so AI can only assist peripheral elements such as blueprint interpretation, predictive diagnostics, or record-keeping. Demand is constrained by building construction volumes, accessibility codes, and mandatory safety inspections rather than installer cost, allowing only modest expansion via more frequent modernizations. Because disruption remains low, the occupation stays resilient even if productivity tools improve.

title: Emergency management directors
rationale: Core work mixes knowledge tasks (hazard assessment, plan drafting, funding applications, damage analysis) that AI can already assist via modeling, simulation, and report generation with irreducible human elements of multi-agency coordination, real-time crisis leadership, on-site command, and interpersonal decision-making under uncertainty. Demand is only moderately elastic: cheaper/faster planning could expand coverage among smaller municipalities and private firms currently constrained by budgets, yet the number of jurisdictions and organizations needing directors remains structurally limited, so productivity gains are only partially absorbed by higher volume. Because disruption stays moderate, AI reshapes peripheral tools without displacing the occupation’s essential human presence and accountability, fitting the resilient category.

title: EMTs and paramedics
rationale: Core EMT/paramedic work is predominantly physical and situational—responding to unpredictable scenes, lifting/moving patients, hands-on life support, and real-time care in chaotic outdoor environments—so AI mainly assists peripheral tasks like documentation, EKG interpretation support, inventory, and dispatch optimization rather than replacing presence or manual skills. Demand is largely inelastic because call volume is driven by fixed real-world incidents (crashes, cardiac events, aging-related emergencies) rather than price or speed; cheaper/faster service may modestly expand rural coverage or community paramedicine but will not multiply total emergencies. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation remains resilient as AI touches the edges without reshaping the essential human-on-scene role.

title: Entertainment and recreation managers
rationale: Core duties mix cognitive planning, budgeting, and strategy with substantial on-site facility oversight, real-time customer engagement, staff leadership, equipment inspection, and safety enforcement that require physical presence and interpersonal judgment; AI already assists program ideation, scheduling, feedback analysis, and budget drafting but leaves the operational and people-facing core intact. Demand for recreation and wellness experiences is growing with demographic and lifestyle trends, so productivity gains can support more programs, facilities, and personalized offerings rather than pure headcount reduction, producing moderate elasticity. Because disruption remains only moderate, the occupation is resilient: AI tools will raise individual productivity on the knowledge-work periphery without reshaping or displacing the essential human role.

title: Environmental engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: Core duties center on physical field and lab work—setting up and operating pollution-control equipment, collecting air/soil/water samples, handling hazardous materials, and conducting on-site inspections—which require human presence and cannot be fully automated, while AI already assists with data analysis, compliance document review, scheduling, and record-keeping, producing only moderate disruption. Demand is moderately elastic: lower costs could expand monitoring frequency, remediation projects, and voluntary compliance amid rising environmental concerns, yet growth remains capped by regulations, public budgets, and the finite stock of polluted sites. With disruption at a moderate level, AI mainly touches peripheral cognitive tasks and the occupation remains resilient overall.

title: Environmental engineers
rationale: Core tasks center on cognitive and digital work—system design, scientific data analysis, modeling, report writing, permit preparation, and technical advising—which AI already accelerates via generative design, simulation, and document tools, producing high disruption even as site inspections and PE-level judgment retain a human role. Elasticity is moderate because dramatically cheaper/faster engineering unlocks more remediation, water/air quality, and climate-resilience projects driven by public awareness and regulation, yet growth remains bounded by capital budgets, construction capacity, and permitting timelines. The occupation therefore restructures: workers who master AI-augmented workflows thrive while pure traditional skill sets face displacement.

title: Environmental science and protection technicians
rationale: Core work mixes substantial physical fieldwork (site inspections, sample collection, equipment setup/maintenance under variable outdoor conditions) with lab analysis and reporting; AI already assists data interpretation, modeling, and report generation but cannot replace on-site presence or hands-on sampling, keeping disruption moderate. Demand has some elasticity because cheaper/faster monitoring could expand proactive testing, impact studies, and coverage in more locations, yet regulatory compliance baselines and public-sector budgets constrain unlimited growth. With disruption at only moderate levels, AI mainly augments peripheral cognitive tasks without reshaping the occupation’s core, fitting the resilient category.

title: Environmental scientists and specialists
rationale: Core tasks center on data analysis, environmental modeling, risk assessment, regulatory compliance documentation, and report writing—predominantly cognitive and digital work where AI tools for geospatial analysis, predictive modeling, and automated reporting are already materially useful and advancing rapidly—while fieldwork and stakeholder interaction remain secondary. Demand is highly elastic because environmental monitoring, climate studies, corporate sustainability consulting, and restoration planning are currently constrained by cost; dramatically cheaper and faster output would unlock substantial latent demand driven by climate pressures, ESG requirements, and public interest. Productivity gains therefore expand total volume of work rather than shrink headcount, enabling specialists to cover more sites, deeper analyses, and proactive projects. This combination of high disruption with high elasticity produces an augment outcome.

title: Epidemiologists
rationale: Core work centers on study design, statistical analysis of large datasets, literature synthesis, report writing, and grant proposals—all predominantly cognitive and digital tasks where AI already accelerates modeling, pattern detection, and drafting, driving high disruption even as fieldwork, community outreach, and policy judgment retain human presence. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster analysis unlocks more surveillance, outbreak modeling, and research on emerging/chronic diseases, yet public-sector budgets and funding cycles limit how fully demand expands. The occupation therefore restructures around AI-augmented analytics and interpretation rather than contracting or remaining unchanged.

title: Exercise physiologists
rationale: Core work mixes cognitive tasks (analyzing medical histories, interpreting test data, designing individualized programs) that AI can already assist with against hands-on requirements (operating medical equipment for stress/endurance tests, real-time vital measurements, in-person program implementation and client coaching) that demand physical presence and interpersonal judgment. This keeps disruption moderate rather than high. Elasticity is moderate because lower cost and faster program design would unlock more preventive and chronic-disease management use among currently underserved populations, yet growth remains tempered by physician referrals, insurance, and clinical settings. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation stays resilient: AI tools will raise productivity on the knowledge side without reshaping or displacing the essential human-delivered core.

title: Farmers, ranchers, and other agricultural managers
rationale: Core tasks mix physical on-site supervision, equipment/facility maintenance, animal care, and real-world problem-solving with cognitive elements like market analysis, crop/livestock decisions, and record-keeping; AI already aids the latter via precision agriculture tools and will deepen optimization, but unpredictable outdoor conditions and hands-on presence keep disruption moderate. Demand for agricultural output is highly inelastic—people do not consume dramatically more food or fiber when production becomes cheaper or faster—so historical productivity gains have driven consolidation and fewer managers rather than expanded headcount. With disruption only moderate, AI primarily augments peripheral analysis and planning without reshaping the occupation's essential real-world core, fitting the resilient category.

title: Fashion designers
rationale: Core tasks such as trend research, ideation, CAD sketching, and generating design variations are predominantly cognitive and digital, and generative AI tools already materially accelerate them, placing disruption in the high range even though fabric selection, prototyping, and production oversight retain physical elements. Elasticity is high because dramatically cheaper and faster design unlocks latent demand for more frequent collections, micro-trends, mass customization, and independent brands, amplified by social media and e-commerce. The combination means AI multiplies output per designer rather than simply displacing headcount, fitting the augment category.

title: Film and video editors and camera operators
rationale: Editing is almost entirely digital and already materially assisted by AI tools for rough cuts, color, effects, and generative video, while camera work retains physical on-location presence, equipment handling, and real-time judgment yet is increasingly aided by robotics, drones, and synthetic media—yielding high overall disruption to core tasks. Demand elasticity is high because video content production has been heavily cost-constrained; dramatically cheaper and faster output unlocks large latent demand across streaming, social, marketing, corporate, and educational media, so far more content gets created. The combination produces an augment outcome: productivity gains expand total output enough that headcount remains stable or grows while the skill mix shifts toward AI orchestration and creative direction.

title: Financial analysts
rationale: Core tasks—evaluating financial statements and data, studying trends, building models/portfolios, and writing recommendation reports—are almost entirely digital/cognitive and already being materially accelerated by AI tools for analysis, forecasting, and drafting, placing the occupation firmly in the very-high disruption band. Human elements such as management-team assessment, client meetings, and final judgment remain, but they no longer dominate daily work. On elasticity, cheaper and faster analysis unlocks meaningful expansion (more assets actively covered, more small firms and retail investors receiving sophisticated advice, deeper risk modeling), yet total demand is still bounded by the finite size of capital markets, regulatory constraints, and institutional decision cycles, producing only moderate net growth in headcount. The combination of high disruption and moderate elasticity therefore implies substantial skill-set restructuring rather than pure replacement or pure augmentation.

title: Financial clerks
rationale: Core tasks—record updates, bill calculation, credit verification, claims/loan/payroll processing, and transaction documentation—are almost entirely digital, cognitive, and language-based, with AI already automating invoice processing, credit checks, and self-service portals as noted by BLS. Physical presence is minimal except for niche roles like gambling cage workers. Demand is highly inelastic: the volume of bills, payrolls, loans, and claims is driven by underlying economic activity rather than processing cost, so 10x productivity gains translate directly into fewer clerks rather than expanded output. This matches the replace category (disruption ≥7, elasticity ≤4) and aligns with the projected 5% employment decline.

title: Financial examiners
rationale: Core duties center on reviewing balance sheets and loan files, analyzing risk and regulatory impact, and drafting safety/soundness reports—predominantly digital cognitive work where AI already accelerates document review, anomaly detection, risk modeling, and report generation, producing a disruption score of 7. Demand is largely fixed by the number of regulated institutions and mandated exam frequency/depth rather than price; cheaper examinations unlock only limited extra coverage of fintechs or deeper continuous monitoring, so elasticity remains low at 4. High disruption paired with low elasticity therefore places the occupation in the replace category, with AI absorbing analytical volume and headcount expected to contract.

title: Financial managers
rationale: Financial managers' core work—preparing statements and forecasts, analyzing market trends, monitoring compliance, and generating reports—is predominantly digital and cognitive, with AI already providing material assistance via automated modeling, anomaly detection, and predictive analytics; strategic advising and supervision remain human-centric but are a shrinking share of daily tasks. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster financial oversight unlocks more sophisticated risk management, cash planning, and analysis for mid-sized firms and new specialties, yet the number of organizations and regulatory structures caps unlimited expansion. High disruption combined with only moderate elasticity means the role persists but shifts heavily toward AI orchestration, judgment, and cross-functional advising, displacing those who cannot adapt.

title: Fire inspectors
rationale: Core work centers on physical onsite building searches, debris sorting at fire scenes under PPE, outdoor patrols, and in-person evidence collection or code enforcement, so AI can only assist peripheral cognitive pieces such as blueprint review, risk modeling, or photo analysis of scenes. Demand is largely fixed by the stock of buildings, regulatory inspection schedules, and the incidence of fires rather than price; cheaper inspections unlock only limited extra frequency or education programs, not a large expansion of total work. Because disruption stays moderate, the occupation remains resilient even if some analytical tasks are automated.

title: Firefighters
rationale: Core firefighter tasks—driving apparatus, operating hoses and ladders, entering burning structures, physical rescues, and hands-on emergency medical care—are overwhelmingly physical, hazardous, and require real-time human presence in unpredictable environments; AI can only touch peripheral elements such as incident reports, training simulations, or predictive risk mapping. Demand is driven by the fixed incidence of fires, medical calls, and mandated public-safety coverage rather than price or speed, so even large productivity gains would not unlock substantial new volume of work. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation remains resilient regardless of modest elasticity.

title: Fishing and hunting workers
rationale: Core tasks—hauling nets and traps, sorting and packing catch, vessel handling in open water, and physical trapping or hunting—are almost entirely manual, outdoor, and dependent on unpredictable real-world conditions, so AI remains peripheral (better sonar/GPS analytics or predictive stock models) and does not reshape daily work. Demand is highly inelastic because total allowable catch is capped by biological stocks, quotas, and regulations; productivity gains simply reduce the labor needed for a fixed harvest rather than expanding output. The occupation therefore stays resilient: AI may improve equipment efficiency at the margin but leaves the physical, presence-based core intact.

title: Fitness trainers and instructors
rationale: Core tasks center on physical demonstration of exercises, real-time observation and correction of client form, in-person motivation, and leading group classes, all of which require human presence and physical fitness; AI already assists peripheral knowledge work such as program design, progress tracking via wearables, nutrition advice, and marketing content, but does not reshape the hands-on core. Demand elasticity is high because personal training and specialized classes remain cost-prohibitive for many, and cheaper/faster delivery (via AI-assisted planning that lets trainers serve more clients) would unlock substantial latent demand driven by obesity, aging, and wellness trends. The net effect is resilient because disruption remains moderate and presence-dependent, so AI augments rather than displaces the occupation even as overall market volume grows.

title: Flight attendants
rationale: Core duties center on physical presence in the aircraft cabin for safety inspections, emergency response, evacuations, passenger assistance, and service, all of which require real-world, unpredictable human intervention and are federally mandated; AI can only touch peripheral elements such as scheduling, training simulations, or automated announcements. Demand is tightly linked to flight volume and fixed regulatory minimums per aircraft, so even large productivity gains would not unlock substantial new consumption of the service itself. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation remains resilient regardless of modest elasticity.

title: Flooring installers and tile and stone setters
rationale: Core tasks—removing old materials, leveling surfaces, cutting and placing tile/carpet/stone with adhesives and tools, grouting, and finishing—are almost entirely physical, on-site, and require strength, kneeling, and real-world adaptation to irregular surfaces, so AI remains irrelevant beyond peripheral estimating or design apps. Demand for installations is driven by housing construction and renovation cycles rather than being heavily suppressed by labor cost alone, so even large productivity gains would produce only limited expansion rather than 10x more floors being laid. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation stays resilient: AI does not reshape the daily work or displace headcount.

title: Floral designers
rationale: Core tasks center on physical handling, cutting, arranging, and on-site setup of perishable flowers plus tactile knowledge of bloom properties and seasons, so AI can only assist peripheral knowledge work such as design inspiration, recommendations, ordering, and admin rather than reshape the hands-on work. Demand is largely fixed by social occasions (weddings, funerals, holidays) and material supply constraints; lower design costs unlock only modest extra everyday or business purchases rather than large volume growth. With disruption remaining moderate, the occupation stays resilient overall.

title: Food and beverage serving and related workers
rationale: Core tasks center on physical presence—greeting, carrying trays, cleaning tables, stocking, and in-person service—which AI cannot perform and only peripherally assists via kiosks, apps, or reservation systems already in use. Demand elasticity is moderate because lower labor costs would expand dining-out frequency, delivery volume, and new outlets, yet total meals remain bounded by human appetite and time. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation stays resilient as AI reshapes only edges of the work.

title: Food preparation workers
rationale: Core tasks—chopping produce and meat, mixing salads, cleaning/sanitizing stations, storing food, and handling physical kitchen equipment—are almost entirely manual and require real-world presence, dexterity, and stamina; AI currently touches only peripheral functions such as inventory tracking or recipe scaling and is unlikely to automate the bulk of hands-on work within a decade. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate because cheaper prep could modestly expand restaurant volume or meal-kit output, yet overall food consumption faces natural limits and is already being reduced by pre-cut supplier ingredients. With disruption well below the high-disruption threshold, the occupation remains resilient: AI does not reshape the core job even if some productivity gains occur.

title: Food processing equipment workers
rationale: Core duties center on physical machine setup, loading ingredients, monitoring gauges in real time, cleaning equipment, and quality checks in noisy, temperature-variable factory floors—tasks that require on-site presence and manual handling rather than digital or language work. AI can optimize recipes, enable predictive maintenance, or automate some sensor-based monitoring and data logging, but these remain peripheral to the hands-on operation of processing lines. Demand for processed food is largely fixed by population size and dietary habits; even large productivity gains from cheaper processing would not unlock dramatically higher consumption volumes, so headcount gains are limited. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation remains resilient overall.

title: Food service managers
rationale: Disruption is moderate because core work mixes on-site physical presence (kitchen oversight, inspections, real-time staffing, customer complaints, safety compliance, and occasional hands-on service) with knowledge tasks; AI already assists scheduling, inventory forecasting, budgeting, and payroll but cannot replace the unpredictable human leadership and physical environment. Elasticity is moderate as productivity gains could enable multi-unit oversight or slightly lower overhead that supports modest restaurant expansion, yet demand remains constrained by consumer dining preferences, real estate, and overall food-service volume rather than exploding. The net effect is resilient since disruption stays at or below 6: AI reshapes admin tools without altering the occupation’s fundamental need for human presence in live food operations.

title: Forensic science technicians
rationale: Core work splits between physical crime-scene collection, photography, evidence handling, and chain-of-custody duties that require unpredictable real-world presence, plus laboratory chemical/biological analysis and report writing; AI already assists image matching, DNA interpretation, ballistics databases, and report drafting but cannot replace sample preparation, scene judgment, or court testimony, placing disruption firmly in the moderate range. Demand is driven by crime volume, police caseloads, and court needs; while lab backlogs and under-use of advanced testing create some latent demand that cheaper AI-assisted analysis could unlock, overall volume remains constrained by budgets, investigation rates, and legal process, yielding only moderate elasticity. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient—AI will change tools and throughput but not reshape the essential human presence and physical-science core.

title: Forest and conservation workers
rationale: Core duties—planting seedlings, clearing brush and trails, cutting diseased trees, spraying, equipment maintenance, and firebreak construction—are almost entirely physical, outdoor, and location-bound in remote terrain, so AI and remote sensing only touch peripheral monitoring or planning tasks rather than the hands-on work itself. Demand is largely fixed by the finite acreage of managed forests, government budgets, and timber/fire-suppression needs; even large productivity gains would not unlock dramatically more reforestation or trail work. Because disruption remains low, the occupation stays resilient: AI may trim some counting or scouting labor but does not reshape the essential physical role.

title: Fundraisers
rationale: Core tasks such as donor research, crafting appeals, digital campaign optimization, record-keeping, and success evaluation are predominantly cognitive, language-based, and already materially assisted by AI tools for personalization, predictive analytics, and content generation, though high-touch relationship building for major gifts and in-person event execution still require human presence. Demand is highly elastic because professional fundraising capacity has long been cost-constrained for smaller nonprofits and under-resourced causes; dramatically cheaper and faster outreach unlocks far more campaigns, personalized solicitations, and total dollars raised across the sector. High disruption combined with high elasticity means AI multiplies each fundraiser’s output while expanding the overall market enough to keep headcount stable or growing for those who adapt to AI-augmented strategy and relationship roles.

title: Funeral service workers
rationale: Core tasks center on physical handling and preparation of remains, in-person removal and site coordination, and high-empathy counseling of grieving families—all of which require unpredictable real-world presence and human interpersonal skills that AI cannot perform. AI can only assist peripheral digital work such as document filing, scheduling, option menus, and obituary drafting. Demand is almost entirely inelastic because the volume of funerals is fixed by mortality rates; making planning or administration 10x cheaper does not cause more deaths or unlock large latent volume, so productivity gains would not expand headcount. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation remains resilient.

title: Gambling services workers
rationale: Core tasks for the bulk of workers (dealers, floor supervisors, runners) center on physical presence at tables or windows, manual handling of cards/chips/tickets, real-time customer interaction, and monitoring unpredictable human behavior—areas where AI remains peripheral (e.g., enhanced surveillance analytics or back-office scheduling). Managers involve more cognitive work but still require on-floor leadership. Demand elasticity is low because gambling volume is constrained by regulation, physical floor space, and social limits on consumption; cheaper or faster operations may enable modest expansion of tables or online products but will not generate proportional headcount growth, as already reflected in BLS projections of flat employment amid online automation.

title: General maintenance and repair workers
rationale: Core tasks center on hands-on physical repair of buildings, machines, plumbing, electrical systems, and equipment using tools in unpredictable real-world settings, so AI only assists peripheral elements like diagnostics from sensors/images, blueprint analysis, cost estimates, supply ordering, and record-keeping. Demand elasticity is low because the stock of buildings and equipment sets a relatively fixed need for upkeep; cheaper or faster work may unlock some deferred maintenance or more frequent preventive service but will not produce dramatically higher total volume. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation remains resilient as AI does not reshape the essential on-site presence and manual work.

title: General office clerks
rationale: Core duties—data entry, document typing/editing, scheduling, phone handling, filing, and bill processing—are predominantly routine digital and language-based tasks already being automated by AI chatbots, document tools, electronic filing systems, and scheduling software, placing the occupation firmly in AI’s path. Demand for general clerical support is largely fixed by organizational size and operational volume rather than price; making the work dramatically cheaper does not unlock proportional new demand for more phone answering or record-keeping. This combination of high disruption and inelastic demand produces net headcount contraction, consistent with the BLS projection of a 7% decline.

title: Genetic counselors
rationale: Disruption is high because core work is predominantly cognitive and language-based—interpreting genetic data, risk assessment, educating clients on complex results, and documentation—areas where AI tools already assist with variant analysis, pedigree generation, literature synthesis, and report drafting, even as empathetic counseling and nuanced decision support still require human presence. Elasticity is high because demand is currently constrained by a severe shortage (only ~4,000 counselors) and cost/access barriers amid exploding genetic testing and precision medicine; making counseling 10x faster/cheaper would unlock far more sessions across prenatal, cancer, and population screening. This combination fits augment: productivity gains expand total output and access enough to keep headcount stable or growing rather than contracting.

title: Geographers
rationale: Core tasks center on GIS analysis, satellite/remote-sensing interpretation, spatial data modeling, map creation, and report writing—predominantly digital/cognitive work already being accelerated by geospatial AI, computer vision, and generative tools—while fieldwork and interviews form a minority of duties for most practitioners. Demand is heavily constrained by federal and state budgets (nearly 80% of employment) plus structural limits on specialized research volume, so 10x productivity gains translate mainly into fewer positions rather than dramatically more studies. This combination of high disruption and low elasticity produces net replacement pressure and headcount contraction.

title: Geological and hydrologic technicians
rationale: Core duties center on physical fieldwork (sample collection with tools/shovels/gauges in remote outdoor sites), equipment installation/maintenance, and hands-on lab testing, which AI cannot perform; AI only assists secondary digital tasks like data compilation, report writing, GIS mapping, and analysis. Demand elasticity is low because resource exploration, water monitoring, and extraction volumes are constrained by geology, energy markets, regulations, and government funding rather than technician cost or speed—productivity gains from AI or drones (already noted by BLS) mostly reduce headcount needs rather than unlock large new volumes of work. With disruption only moderate, the occupation remains resilient as AI reshapes peripheral analysis without displacing the human presence required for core tasks.

title: Geoscientists
rationale: AI already materially accelerates core cognitive tasks such as seismic/remote-sensing interpretation, geologic modeling, GIS mapping, sample data analysis, and report writing, which occupy a large share of office and lab time, yet essential fieldwork—sample collection, on-site surveys, and remote expeditions—remains irreducibly physical and presence-dependent, producing high-but-not-maximal disruption. Cheaper, faster geoscience output would unlock additional exploration, environmental-assessment, and hazard-mapping projects, yet demand remains bounded by commodity markets, capital-intensive drilling/permitting, and regulatory budgets, so elasticity is only moderate. Because disruption sits at the upper edge of the moderate range, the occupation is classified resilient: AI reshapes tools and productivity without eliminating the need for human geoscientists.

title: Glaziers
rationale: Glaziers' core work is almost entirely physical—measuring, cutting, lifting, and fastening heavy glass on-site, often at heights and outdoors—which AI cannot perform and will not meaningfully automate within 10 years; any AI role is limited to peripheral blueprint interpretation or design optimization. Demand for glass installation is driven by construction and repair cycles with only modest expansion potential if costs fall, constrained by overall building activity rather than latent unmet need. Because disruption remains low, the occupation is resilient to AI-driven change.

title: Graphic designers
rationale: Graphic design is almost entirely digital knowledge work centered on software-driven creation of layouts, logos, illustrations, and visual concepts, tasks already materially accelerated by generative AI tools like image models and automated design platforms, matching the very-high disruption examples. Demand elasticity is high because dramatically cheaper and faster design unlocks substantial latent demand from small businesses, marketers, content platforms, and product teams that previously skipped professional work or relied on templates, expanding total visual output rather than merely shrinking headcount. The combination of disruption >=7 and elasticity >=7 produces an augment outcome in which AI multiplies each designer's productivity while overall volume of design work grows enough to stabilize or increase employment for those who adapt.

title: Grounds maintenance workers
rationale: Core tasks—mowing, planting, pruning, pesticide application, and equipment operation—are almost entirely physical, outdoor, and require real-world presence and manual dexterity, so AI remains peripheral (scheduling apps, plant-ID tools, or early robotic mowers) and does not reshape daily work. Demand for grounds care has some price sensitivity—cheaper service could shift more homeowners from DIY and support expanded green spaces—but is structurally capped by finite land area, weather seasons, and institutional budgets, limiting large-scale expansion. Because disruption stays low, the occupation is resilient: AI may trim admin edges or enable modest productivity gains without displacing the bulk of hands-on labor.

title: Hand laborers and material movers
rationale: Core tasks are overwhelmingly physical and manual—lifting, packing by hand, cleaning vehicles, stocking shelves, and collecting refuse—which require real-world presence and physical stamina that AI cannot perform, so disruption remains low even as AI assists with peripheral scanning, inventory tracking, or route optimization. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster material handling would expand e-commerce order volumes, warehouse throughput, and retail restocking, partially absorbing productivity gains, though structural limits on physical goods movement prevent unlimited growth. The net effect is resilient since disruption stays well below the threshold that would reshape the occupation itself.

title: Hazardous materials removal workers
rationale: Core tasks center on physical presence in variable, often confined or outdoor sites—building containment, scraping/vacuuming materials, operating heavy equipment, packaging waste, and wearing full PPE—which AI and robotics can only peripherally assist via planning, sensor-based detection, or record-keeping over the next decade. Demand is largely fixed by regulatory mandates, the finite stock of legacy contaminants (asbestos, lead, nuclear sites), and sporadic funding rather than price; cheaper/faster work unlocks only modest additional cleanups. Because disruption remains low, the occupation stays resilient with AI touching admin and diagnostics but not reshaping headcount or core fieldwork.

title: Health and safety engineers
rationale: Core work mixes knowledge tasks (plan review, regulation interpretation, accident analysis, safety program design) that AI can already assist via compliance tools, simulation, and report generation with physical on-site inspections, hazard observation, and interpersonal investigations that still require human presence and judgment. Demand is largely set by regulatory floors, facility counts, and compliance needs rather than latent consumer appetite, so large productivity gains would mostly reduce headcount rather than unlock dramatically more safety engineering work. Because disruption remains moderate, the occupation is resilient overall.

title: Health education specialists
rationale: Core work centers on knowledge tasks—assessing needs via data, developing educational materials and programs, evaluating outcomes, grant writing, and advocacy—which AI already accelerates through content generation, analytics, personalization, and drafting. Human presence remains essential for live instruction, community trust-building, and interpersonal facilitation, but these are increasingly AI-augmented rather than AI-proof. Demand is highly elastic because prevention education is chronically under-supplied due to cost; dramatically cheaper, scalable materials and outreach would expand workplace wellness programs, public campaigns, insurer initiatives, and underserved-community coverage far beyond current budgets. High disruption plus high elasticity therefore yields augmentation: specialists oversee far more output with stable or growing headcount.

title: Health information technologists and medical registrars
rationale: Core tasks—abstracting clinical data from records, assigning codes, maintaining registries, validating integrity, compiling reports, and analyzing outcomes—are almost entirely digital and cognitive, placing them squarely in AI’s path via NLP, automated coding, and analytics tools that already assist EHR work and medical registries. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper/faster analysis unlocks more thorough quality tracking, research use, and registry coverage across more organizations, yet overall volume remains constrained by patient numbers, regulatory reporting mandates, and healthcare budgets rather than expanding without limit. High disruption combined with only moderate elasticity means the occupation persists but shifts toward AI oversight, system design, compliance judgment, and higher-level interpretation, requiring substantial skill adaptation.

title: Heating, air conditioning, and refrigeration mechanics and installers
rationale: Core work is overwhelmingly physical and site-based—installing equipment, soldering pipes, handling refrigerants, working in cramped spaces, and performing hands-on repairs—so AI can only assist peripheral tasks such as load calculations, remote diagnostics, scheduling, or record-keeping. This places disruption firmly in the low range, comparable to electricians or plumbers. Elasticity is limited because the stock of buildings and systems largely fixes demand; cheaper service may unlock modest extra maintenance or efficiency upgrades but will not produce order-of-magnitude expansion. With disruption well below 7, the occupation remains resilient: AI tools will improve productivity at the margin without reshaping the occupation’s fundamental skill set or headcount trajectory.

title: Heavy and tractor-trailer truck drivers
rationale: Core tasks center on physical vehicle operation, cargo securing, inspections, and real-world road presence amid unpredictable traffic, weather, and conditions, so AI currently only assists peripheral elements like electronic logging, GPS routing, predictive maintenance, and ADAS safety features without replacing the driver. Full highway autonomy is advancing but faces regulatory, liability, and edge-case barriers that keep human presence essential over a 10-year horizon. Freight demand shows moderate elasticity because lower transport costs can expand e-commerce volumes and just-in-time shipping, yet overall ton-miles remain constrained by goods production, infrastructure, and GDP growth rather than exploding. This keeps disruption moderate and the occupation resilient, with AI touching support tasks while headcount tracks broader economic demand for goods movement.

title: Heavy vehicle and mobile equipment service technicians
rationale: Core work remains predominantly physical—disassembling/reassembling heavy components, on-site repairs of engines/hydraulics, lifting, welding, and tool use—which AI cannot perform, though AI already assists and will further improve computerized diagnostics, predictive maintenance, manuals, and logging. Demand for service is largely derived from the fixed stock of construction, farm, and rail equipment in use; cheaper/faster repairs enable modestly better utilization or preventive work but do not unlock large latent demand, as equipment fleets grow with economic activity rather than repair cost. With disruption only moderate, the occupation stays resilient: AI augments peripheral cognitive tasks without reshaping the hands-on core or driving major headcount contraction.

title: High school teachers
rationale: AI already materially assists core cognitive tasks such as lesson planning, content generation, assessment design, grading, and adaptive materials, which form a large share of teachers’ non-classroom work, and the trajectory points to deeper integration into instruction itself, placing the occupation in the high-disruption range even though real-time classroom management and relational presence remain human. Demand elasticity is only moderate because the stock of high-school-age students is demographically fixed and public-school funding formulas constrain rapid expansion, yet cheaper high-quality instruction can still unlock more electives, smaller effective class sizes, remediation, and adult secondary programs in some segments. The combination produces a restructure outcome: headcount need not collapse, but the skill mix shifts sharply toward AI orchestration, facilitation, and socio-emotional work, so non-adapters are displaced while adapters thrive.

title: Historians
rationale: Core historian work—gathering and analyzing documents, interpreting significance, and writing reports/books—is predominantly cognitive and language-based, with AI already accelerating literature search, source synthesis, pattern detection in digitized archives, and draft generation; physical artifact handling and site visits remain secondary for many roles. Demand elasticity is moderate because institutional funding (government, museums, societies) and fixed scholarly niches limit expansion, yet cheaper output can unlock more popular history content, corporate/public-history consulting, educational materials, and niche research that was previously cost-prohibitive. High disruption paired with only moderate demand growth means the occupation persists but requires substantial skill shifts toward AI orchestration, original interpretive judgment, public engagement, and curation of non-digitized sources.

title: Home health and personal care aides
rationale: Core duties—bathing, dressing, lifting/transferring clients, housekeeping, meal prep, and in-person companionship—are overwhelmingly physical, manual, and require unpredictable real-world presence and emotional labor; AI can only touch peripheral tasks such as scheduling, basic record-keeping, or remote sensor alerts. Demand elasticity is high because professional home care is currently cost-constrained for many families and the aging population; dramatically cheaper or more available care would unlock substantial latent hours of service and shift more unpaid family caregiving into the formal market. With disruption well below the threshold for structural change, the occupation remains resilient: AI may improve efficiency at the margins but will not reshape the headcount trajectory driven by demographics.

title: Human resources managers
rationale: HR managers' core work is predominantly knowledge-based—workforce planning, recruiting strategy, analytics, policy design, compliance, and benefits oversight—where AI already automates resume screening, data analysis, drafting, and admin, materially changing daily tasks even if interpersonal mediation and executive consulting remain human. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper AI-augmented HR unlocks more sophisticated talent practices for mid-sized and smaller firms, yet overall demand is still constrained by organizational headcount ratios and fixed company structures rather than exploding. This combination means the role persists but requires substantial skill shifts toward AI orchestration and higher-level strategy, fitting restructure rather than pure replacement or augmentation.

title: Human resources specialists
rationale: Core HR work is predominantly knowledge- and language-based (resume screening, job posting, paperwork, initial outreach, compliance tracking, data analysis), with AI tools already materially used in ATS systems, chatbots, and candidate ranking, so disruption is high even though final interviews and employee-relations judgment still require humans. Elasticity is only moderate because cheaper/faster recruiting and admin unlocks some latent demand from smaller firms and more sophisticated talent programs, yet overall volume remains tightly linked to employment levels and regulatory needs rather than expanding unboundedly. This combination produces a restructure outcome: routine transactional HR shrinks while remaining specialists shift toward strategic, interpersonal, and AI-oversight skills.

title: Hydrologists
rationale: Disruption is moderate because core duties mix essential physical fieldwork (streamflow measurement, sample collection, remote site visits requiring stamina and presence) with knowledge tasks (modeling, data analysis, forecasting, report writing) where AI already assists via remote sensing, complex dataset processing, and simulation tools. Elasticity is low because demand is largely set by government budgets, regulatory requirements, and a finite set of water projects or climate threats; cheaper/faster analysis unlocks some additional monitoring or consulting but does not create dramatically more work. Net effect is resilient as AI remains peripheral to the occupation’s unavoidable real-world presence and does not meet the high-disruption threshold for replacement or restructuring.

title: Industrial designers
rationale: Core tasks such as ideation, sketching, digital rendering, CAD modeling, generative optimization, and usability analysis are predominantly cognitive/digital and already being materially accelerated by generative AI and CAID tools, even though physical prototyping, manufacturing constraints, and client collaboration still require human presence. Cheaper and faster design unlocks substantial latent demand: more product variants, faster iteration cycles, mass customization, and design access for smaller firms and startups that previously could not afford professional industrial design. Productivity gains are therefore absorbed by expanded output rather than pure headcount reduction, so the occupation is augmented rather than replaced.

title: Industrial engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: Core tasks center on statistical production studies, workflow design, cost analysis, layout optimization, and chart/diagram preparation—predominantly cognitive and digital work already assisted by CAD/CAM, process-mining tools, and simulation software, with AI trajectory (digital twins, computer vision for time-motion studies, generative optimization) making further automation highly feasible over 10 years; residual on-site observation and staff coordination prevent a higher score. Elasticity is moderate because dramatically cheaper analysis unlocks more frequent process-improvement projects and broader adoption by smaller manufacturers, yet total demand remains constrained by the finite base of production facilities and physical output volumes rather than expanding without bound. High disruption paired with only moderate demand growth means the occupation persists but requires substantial skill shifts toward AI tool orchestration and human-factors implementation, displacing non-adapters.

title: Industrial engineers
rationale: Industrial engineering is predominantly knowledge work centered on data collection/analysis, process simulation, system design, and optimization recommendations—tasks where AI tools for analytics, generative design, and predictive modeling are already materially useful and will deepen further—though real-world observation of factories/hospitals and cross-functional collaboration keep it from being fully digital. Demand elasticity is high because efficiency and cost-reduction needs are currently constrained by the expense of skilled IE time; 10x cheaper/faster output unlocks far more process redesigns, supply-chain optimizations, and automation projects across manufacturing, healthcare, and logistics. High disruption paired with high elasticity means productivity gains expand total work volume enough that headcount remains stable or grows as each engineer covers far more systems.

title: Industrial machinery mechanics, machinery maintenance workers, and millwrights
rationale: Core duties—disassembling, repairing, calibrating, installing, and moving industrial machinery—are overwhelmingly physical, on-site, and require manual dexterity, welding, and real-world mechanical troubleshooting that AI cannot execute. AI already aids peripheral elements such as predictive diagnostics, vibration analysis, and manual interpretation, but these remain secondary to hands-on work, keeping disruption low. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster maintenance (via better AI tools) can support wider adoption of automated factory equipment and reduce downtime costs, expanding some demand in line with manufacturing growth, yet overall volume is still constrained by the physical stock of industrial plant rather than unlimited latent need. With disruption well below the threshold that reshapes the occupation, the net effect is resilient.

title: Industrial production managers
rationale: Industrial production managers blend analytical planning, data review, and process optimization with on-site floor presence, worker leadership, safety oversight, and real-time physical problem-solving; AI already aids scheduling, predictive analytics, and reporting but cannot replace the human presence and interpersonal core, keeping disruption moderate. Demand for the role is constrained by the capital intensity of manufacturing plants, overall goods-market size, and structural factors such as automation trends and global competition, so even large productivity gains are unlikely to unlock dramatically more manager headcount. The occupation therefore remains resilient: AI reshapes peripheral knowledge tasks without displacing the essential human and physical elements of plant management.

title: Information clerks
rationale: Core tasks—data collection and recording, preparing standard reports/responses, answering routine queries, electronic filing, and processing applications/orders—are almost entirely digital, language-based, and procedural, already being automated by chatbots, RPA, document AI, self-service kiosks, and online systems; physical presence is limited to a minority of subtypes (e.g., some hotel or ticket agents) and is itself being eroded by the same tools. Demand for these support functions is largely fixed by external volumes (guests, applicants, court cases, orders) that do not expand when processing becomes cheaper or faster, so productivity gains translate directly into fewer workers rather than more output. This combination of very high disruption and inelastic demand produces net replacement and headcount contraction, consistent with the already-projected decline.

title: Information security analysts
rationale: Core tasks—network monitoring, vulnerability scanning, threat research, report writing, standards development, and recovery planning—are almost entirely digital and cognitive, already being reshaped by AI-driven anomaly detection, automated scanners, log analysis, and generative tools that handle routine detection and drafting. Demand elasticity is high because security investment is currently suppressed by cost and talent shortages; 10x cheaper/faster analysis would unlock continuous monitoring, broader coverage for SMEs, securing of expanding attack surfaces (cloud, IoT, AI systems themselves), and response to AI-powered threats, expanding total output substantially. This combination means AI multiplies each analyst’s productivity while overall demand grows enough to keep headcount stable or rising, placing the occupation in the augment category.

title: Instructional coordinators
rationale: Core tasks such as curriculum design, educational material development, student data analysis, textbook review, and generating training content are predominantly cognitive and language-based, already materially assisted by generative AI and analytics tools, even as classroom observation, mentoring, and staff workshops retain human presence requirements. Demand elasticity is moderate because lower costs could unlock more frequent curriculum updates, specialized programs (e.g., ESL, AI literacy), and support for under-resourced districts, yet overall consumption remains capped by fixed school systems, public budgets, and regulatory standards. High disruption combined with only moderate expansion means the occupation persists but shifts heavily toward AI orchestration, implementation coaching, and interpersonal leadership, displacing those who do not adapt.

title: Insulation workers
rationale: Core tasks—measuring, cutting, spraying, stapling, and securing insulation in walls, attics, pipes, and confined spaces—are almost entirely physical, manual, and site-specific, requiring strength, dexterity, and real-world presence that AI cannot perform; AI only peripherally assists blueprint review or material calculations. Demand for insulation is somewhat cost-sensitive due to energy-efficiency retrofits and new construction, so cheaper/faster work could unlock modest additional volume, but growth remains constrained by housing starts, building stock, and capital budgets rather than expanding unboundedly. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation stays resilient as AI does not reshape the hands-on core.

title: Insurance sales agents
rationale: Core tasks such as analyzing client financial situations and existing coverage, explaining policy features, customizing recommendations, and maintaining records are predominantly cognitive, language-based, and digital; AI recommendation engines, generative chatbots, and automated outreach already materially assist or replace large portions of this work, with rapid further progress expected. Human elements of trust-building and complex negotiation remain but form a shrinking share of daily activity. Demand for insurance itself is driven mainly by regulation, asset ownership, and risk needs rather than the cost or speed of the sales process, so 10x productivity gains unlock only limited additional volume (some optional products and underserved niches) and are largely absorbed by fewer agents plus direct-to-consumer AI channels. This combination of high disruption and low elasticity produces net headcount contraction.

title: Insurance underwriters
rationale: Core tasks—analyzing applications, scoring risk from data/credit/medical records, reviewing automated recommendations, and setting premiums—are almost entirely digital and cognitive, already heavily assisted by underwriting software, and squarely in AI’s path for further automation of pattern recognition and decision rules. Demand for underwriting decisions is largely tied to the existing volume of insurance applications and policies, which is not strongly suppressed by underwriting cost or speed; modest gains in product variety or access will not offset large productivity increases. High disruption combined with low elasticity therefore produces net headcount contraction, consistent with the BLS projection of declining employment.

title: Interior designers
rationale: Core tasks like space planning, CAD/BIM drafting, material specification, cost estimation, and concept visualization are predominantly digital/cognitive and already being transformed by generative AI tools that produce floor plans, 3D renders, and mood boards in minutes, though client consultation, site visits, contractor coordination, and code-compliant installation oversight still require human presence. Demand elasticity is moderate because dramatically cheaper design unlocks latent projects from homeowners and small firms who currently DIY or skip professionals, plus more frequent redesigns, yet total volume remains constrained by physical construction costs, materials, and renovation budgets that AI does not reduce. This combination means the occupation persists with expanded output but requires substantial skill shifts toward AI orchestration, client relationship management, and real-world execution, fitting restructure rather than pure replacement or pure augmentation.

title: Interpreters and translators
rationale: Core tasks are predominantly language conversion—written translation is already heavily assisted by CAT tools and machine translation with post-editing, while real-time interpreting and sign language remain more human-dependent but are seeing rapid AI speech-to-speech advances—placing the occupation in the high-disruption knowledge-work range. Elasticity is only moderate because cheaper/faster output unlocks more localization, content, and access services, yet regulatory requirements (courts, healthcare), quality/cultural stakes, and fixed institutional demand prevent unlimited expansion. High disruption plus moderate elasticity means the occupation persists but shifts toward specialized post-editing, high-stakes interpreting, and cultural nuance work, displacing those who do not adapt.

title: Ironworkers
rationale: Ironworkers' core tasks—unloading and positioning steel, signaling cranes, cutting/bending/welding, aligning at heights, and bolting in outdoor conditions—are almost entirely physical, manual, and site-specific, requiring strength, balance, and real-world presence that AI cannot replace. AI may aid peripheral elements like blueprint interpretation or safety monitoring, but does not meaningfully alter daily work today or in the near trajectory. Demand is tied to fixed infrastructure and commercial construction volumes constrained by capital, regulation, and land rather than being heavily suppressed by labor cost, so productivity gains would not unlock large expansion. With low disruption, the occupation is resilient regardless of modest elasticity.

title: Janitors and building cleaners
rationale: Core duties—emptying trash, mopping, restroom cleaning, disinfecting, minor repairs, and securing buildings—are almost entirely physical, on-site, and require real-world presence and manual labor, so AI affects only peripheral tasks like supply ordering or scheduling. Demand for cleaning is largely fixed by the existing stock of buildings, occupancy, and hygiene standards; even large productivity gains would not unlock dramatically more cleaning volume. Because disruption remains low, the occupation is resilient to AI-driven change over the next decade.

title: Jewelers and precious stone and metal workers
rationale: Core tasks center on manual craftsmanship—soldering, stone setting, polishing, repairs, and metal shaping—that demand physical dexterity, near vision, and real-world presence at a workbench, even though AI already aids peripheral digital elements such as generative CAD design, computer-vision gem grading, and appraisal reports. Demand for jewelry remains constrained by discretionary consumer spending, fixed material costs of precious metals and stones, and fashion cycles, so productivity gains produce only modest expansion in custom or repair work rather than large volume growth. Because disruption stays moderate, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes design and analysis tools but leaves the hands-on production core largely intact.

title: Judges and hearing officers
rationale: Core duties center on presiding over hearings, real-time evaluation of arguments, ensuring procedural fairness, and issuing authoritative judgments that carry legal and societal legitimacy—tasks that require human presence, accountability, and institutional authority AI cannot assume. AI will materially assist research, document analysis, and opinion drafting, altering the knowledge-work portions, but this remains mixed rather than transformative of the role. Demand is structurally capped by government budgets, fixed judicial positions, appointment/election processes, and caseload volumes that do not freely expand with lower cost or higher speed, so productivity gains translate more to throughput than headcount growth. The combination yields a resilient occupation where AI remains peripheral to the essential human function.

title: Kindergarten and elementary school teachers
rationale: Core daily work centers on in-person instruction, real-time classroom management, behavioral supervision, social-emotional coaching, and physical presence with young children—tasks that remain largely non-digital and unpredictable—while AI already meaningfully assists peripheral knowledge work such as lesson planning, worksheet generation, grading, and adaptive content, producing only moderate overall disruption. Demand is low-elasticity because teacher headcount is driven by fixed student demographics, compulsory attendance, and regulated class sizes rather than price or speed; productivity gains are more likely to enable modestly larger classes or better quality within existing enrollment than to unlock dramatically higher total consumption of elementary teaching services. The occupation therefore remains resilient: AI reshapes tools and admin workflows but does not displace the fundamental human presence required.

title: Labor relations specialists
rationale: Core work is predominantly cognitive and language-based—drafting collective bargaining agreements and policies, analyzing labor law and grievances, preparing negotiation strategies, and generating training materials—where current AI tools already accelerate research, document generation, and compliance checks, with further trajectory toward deeper automation of analysis and prep. Demand remains structurally constrained by union density, the fixed volume of workplace disputes, and collective bargaining cycles; cheaper/faster service unlocks only modest latent use by smaller employers or proactive HR rather than dramatic expansion. High disruption paired with low elasticity therefore implies headcount contraction as productivity gains reduce the number of specialists needed for existing caseloads.

title: Landscape architects
rationale: Landscape architecture is predominantly knowledge and design work centered on CADD modeling, GIS analysis, site planning, cost estimation, and environmental assessment—tasks where generative AI and automation tools are already materially useful and will deepen rapidly—while site inspections and client coordination remain human. Demand elasticity is only moderate because cheaper, faster designs can expand professional work into more residential, green-roof, and restoration projects, yet overall volume remains constrained by physical construction budgets, land availability, and municipal capital spending. High disruption combined with moderate elasticity means the occupation persists but requires substantial skill shifts toward AI-augmented design oversight and ecological judgment, displacing those who do not adapt.

title: Lawyers
rationale: Core lawyer tasks—legal research, analysis of statutes and case law, document drafting (contracts, briefs, wills), and interpretation of regulations—are predominantly cognitive and language-based; AI tools already materially accelerate and automate large portions of this work, even if courtroom advocacy, client counseling, and ethical judgment still require human presence. Demand elasticity is low because while cheaper legal services would unlock some latent access-to-justice demand among individuals and small businesses, growth is capped by court capacity, unauthorized-practice-of-law rules, and the fact that most high-stakes legal needs are not highly price-elastic. The combination of high disruption and limited demand expansion implies significant headcount contraction, especially among junior associates performing routine knowledge work, fitting the replace category.

title: Librarians and library media specialists
rationale: Librarians' work mixes digital knowledge tasks (cataloging, database management, research assistance, material selection) that AI already assists with via search tools, recommenders, and chatbots, against core requirements for physical presence, in-person patron help, children's programming, and community events that AI cannot replace. This yields moderate disruption overall. Demand elasticity is low because library services are constrained by public/school budgets, fixed institutional footprints, and limited latent appetite for 10x more story times or reference sessions; productivity gains therefore translate more to efficiency than expanded headcount. The net effect is resilient as AI reshapes peripheral information tasks without displacing the human-centered core.

title: Library technicians and assistants
rationale: Core duties such as cataloguing, database maintenance, routine reference questions, interlibrary loans, patron registration, and clerical work are predominantly digital, cognitive, and language-based; AI chatbots, automated cataloguing systems, and self-service tools already handle large portions of these and will expand rapidly. Physical tasks like reshelving and in-person program support remain but constitute a shrinking share of the role. Demand is highly inelastic because library usage is already declining due to digital alternatives, public budgets are fixed or constrained, and cheaper staffing does not unlock substantially more patronage or new libraries. High disruption combined with low elasticity therefore points to headcount contraction as AI absorbs the bulk of the work without offsetting demand growth.

title: Licensed practical and licensed vocational nurses
rationale: Core LPN/LVN work centers on hands-on physical care (bathing, bandaging, feeding, vitals checks), direct patient interaction, and real-time presence in homes or facilities; AI can automate charting, flag alerts from sensors, and assist reporting, but these remain peripheral to the occupation’s essential tasks. Demand is shaped by aging demographics and chronic illness prevalence, so lower costs could modestly expand home-health and long-term-care volume, yet overall patient numbers and regulatory staffing ratios constrain unlimited growth. Because disruption stays moderate, the occupation is resilient: AI tools improve efficiency at the edges without displacing or fundamentally rewriting the role.

title: Loan officers
rationale: Core tasks center on gathering/verifying financial data, underwriting analysis, compliance review, and generating recommendations—already heavily software-assisted and squarely in AI’s path for document processing, risk scoring, and decision support—while sales and client conversations remain human but secondary for many roles.
